pope: A, as its first of letters, every speech maintains; The "Primal Deity" is first through all the world's domains
drewLazarus: As the letter A is the first of all letters, so the eternal God is first in the world

pope: No fruit have men of all their studied lore, Save they the 'Purely Wise One's' feet adore
drewLazarus: What Profit have those derived from learning, who worship not the good feet of Him who is possessed of pure knowledge ?

pope: His feet, 'Who o'er the full-blown flower hath past,' who gainIn bliss long time shall dwell above this earthly plain
drewLazarus: They who are united to the glorious feet of Him who passes swiftly over the flower of the mind, shall flourish long above all worlds

pope: His foot, 'Whom want affects not, irks not grief,' who gainShall not, through every time, of any woes complain
drewLazarus: To those who meditate the feet of Him who is void of desire or aversion, evil shall never come

pope: The men, who on the 'King's' true praised delight to dwell, Affects not them the fruit of deeds done ill or well
drewLazarus: The two-fold deeds that spring from darkness shall not adhere to those who delight in the true praise of God

pope: Long live they blest, who 've stood in path from falsehood freed; His, 'Who quenched lusts that from the sense-gates five proceed'
drewLazarus: Those shall long proposer who abide in the faultless way of Him who has destroyed the five desires of the senses

pope: Unless His foot, 'to Whom none can compare,' men gain,'Tis hard for mind to find relief from anxious pain
drewLazarus: Anxiety of mind cannot be removed, except from those who are united to the feet of Him who is incomparable

pope: Unless His feet 'the Sea of Good, the Fair and Bountiful,' men gain,'Tis hard the further bank of being's changeful sea to attain
drewLazarus: None can swim the sea of vice, but those who are united to the feet of that gracious Being who is a sea of virtue

pope: Before His foot, 'the Eight-fold Excellence,' with unbent head, Who stands, like palsied sense, is to all living functions dead
drewLazarus: The head that worships not the feet of Him who is possessed of eight attributes, is as useless as a sense without the power of sensation

pope: They swim the sea of births, the 'Monarch's' foot who gain; None others reach the shore of being's mighty main
drewLazarus: None can swim the great sea of births but those who are united to the feet of God

pope: The world its course maintains through life that rain unfailing gives; Thus rain is known the true ambrosial food of all that lives
drewLazarus: By the continuance of rain the world is preserved in existence; it is therefore worthy to be called ambrosia

pope: The rain makes pleasant food for eaters rise; As food itself, thirst-quenching draught supplies
drewLazarus: Rain produces good food, and is itself food

pope: If clouds, that promised rain, deceive, and in the sky remain, Famine, sore torment, stalks o'er earth's vast ocean-girdled plain
drewLazarus: If the cloud, withholding rain, deceive (our hopes) hunger will long distress the sea-girt spacious world

pope: If clouds their wealth of waters fail on earth to pour, The ploughers plough with oxen's sturdy team no more
drewLazarus: If the abundance of wealth imparting rain diminish, the labour of the plough must cease

pope: 'Tis rain works all: it ruin spreads, then timely aid supplies; As, in the happy days before, it bids the ruined rise
drewLazarus: Rain by its absence ruins men; and by its existence restores them to fortune

pope: If from the clouds no drops of rain are shed'Tis rare to see green herb lift up its head
drewLazarus: If no drop falls from the clouds, not even the green blade of grass will be seen

pope: If clouds restrain their gifts and grant no rain, The treasures fail in ocean's wide domain
drewLazarus: Even the wealth of the wide sea will be diminished, if the cloud that has drawn (its waters) up gives them not back again (in rain)

pope: If heaven grow dry, with feast and offering never more, Will men on earth the heavenly ones adore
drewLazarus: If the heaven dry up, neither yearly festivals, nor daily worship will be offered in this world, to the celestials

pope: If heaven its watery treasures ceases to dispense, Through the wide world cease gifts, and deeds of 'penitence'
drewLazarus: If rain fall not, penance and alms-deeds will not dwell within this spacious world

pope: When water fails, functions of nature cease, you say; Thus when rain fails, no men can walk in 'duty's ordered way'
drewLazarus: If it be said that the duties of life cannot be discharged by any person without water, so without rain there cannot be the flowing of water

pope: The settled rule of every code requires, as highest good, Their greatness who, renouncing all, true to their rule have stood
drewLazarus: The end and aim of all treatise is to extol beyond all other excellence, the greatness of those who, while abiding in the rule of conduct peculiar to their state, have abandoned all desire

pope: As counting those that from the earth have passed away,'Tis vain attempt the might of holy men to say
drewLazarus: To describe the measure of the greatness of those who have forsaken the two-fold desires, is like counting the dead

pope: Their greatness earth transcends, who, way of both worlds weighed, In this world take their stand, in virtue's robe arrayed
drewLazarus: The greatness of those who have discovered the properties of both states of being, and renounced the world, shines forth on earth (beyond all others)

pope: He, who with firmness, curb the five restrains, Is seed for soil of yonder happy plains
drewLazarus: He who guides his five senses by the hook of wisdom will be a seed in the world of heaven

pope: Their might who have destroyed 'the five', shall soothly tellIndra, the lord of those in heaven's wide realms that dwell
drewLazarus: Indra, the king of the inhabitants of the spacious heaven, is himself, a sufficient proof of the strength of him who has subdued his five senses

pope: Things hard in the doing will great men do; Things hard in the doing the mean eschew
drewLazarus: The great will do those things which is difficult to be done; but the mean cannot do them

pope: Taste, light, touch, sound, and smell: who knows the wayOf all the five,- the world submissive owns his sway
drewLazarus: The world is within the knowledge of him who knows the properties of taste, sight, touch, hearing and smell

pope: The might of men whose word is never vain, The 'secret word' shall to the earth proclaim
drewLazarus: The hidden words of the men whose words are full of effect, will shew their greatness to the world

pope: The wrath 'tis hard e'en for an instant to endure, Of those who virtue's hill have scaled, and stand secure
drewLazarus: The anger of those who have ascended the mountain of goodness, though it continue but for a moment, cannot be resisted

pope: Towards all that breathe, with seemly graciousness adorned they live; And thus to virtue's sons the name of 'Anthanar' men give
drewLazarus: The virtuous are truly called Anthanar; because in their conduct towards all creatures they are clothed in kindness

pope: It yields distinction, yields prosperity; what gainGreater than virtue can a living man obtain
drewLazarus: Virtue will confer heaven and wealth; what greater source of happiness can man possess ?

pope: No greater gain than virtue aught can cause; No greater loss than life oblivious of her laws
drewLazarus: There can be no greater source of good than (the practice of) virtue; there can be no greater source of evil than the forgetfulness of it

pope: To finish virtue's work with ceaseless effort strive, What way thou may'st, where'er thou see'st the work may thrive
drewLazarus: As much as possible, in every way, incessantly practise virtue

pope: Spotless be thou in mind! This only merits virtue's name; All else, mere pomp of idle sound, no real worth can claim
drewLazarus: Let him who does virtuous deeds be of spotless mind; to that extent is virtue; all else is vain show

pope: 'Tis virtue when, his footsteps sliding not through envy, wrath, Lust, evil speech-these four, man onwards moves in ordered path
drewLazarus: That conduct is virtue which is free from these four things, viz, malice, desire, anger and bitter speech

pope: Do deeds of virtue now Say not, 'To-morrow we'll be wise'; Thus, when thou diest, shalt thou find a help that never dies
drewLazarus: Defer not virtue to another day; receive her now; and at the dying hour she will be your undying friend

pope: Needs not in words to dwell on virtue's fruits: compareThe man in litter borne with them that toiling bear
drewLazarus: The fruit of virtue need not be described in books; it may be inferred from seeing the bearer of a palanquin and the rider therein

pope: If no day passing idly, good to do each day you toil, A stone it will be to block the way of future days of moil
drewLazarus: If one allows no day to pass without some good being done, his conduct will be a stone to block up the passage to other births

pope: What from virtue floweth, yieldeth dear delight; All else extern, is void of glory's light
drewLazarus: Only that pleasure which flows from domestic virtue is pleasure; all else is not pleasure, and it is without praise

pope: 'Virtue' sums the things that should be done;'Vice' sums the things that man should shun
drewLazarus: That is virtue which each ought to do, and that is vice which each should shun

pope: The men of household virtue, firm in way of good, sustainThe other orders three that rule professed maintain
drewLazarus: He will be called a (true) householder, who is a firm support to the virtuous of the three orders in

pope: To anchorites, to indigent, to those who've passed away, The man for household virtue famed is needful held and stay
drewLazarus: He will be said to flourish in domestic virtue who aids the forsaken, the poor, and the dead

pope: The manes, God, guests kindred, self, in due degree, These five to cherish well is chiefest charity
drewLazarus: The chief (duty of the householder) is to preserve the five-fold rule (of conduct) towards the manes, the Gods, his guests, his relations and himself

pope: Who shares his meal with other, while all guilt he shuns, His virtuous line unbroken though the ages runs
drewLazarus: His descendants shall never fail who, living in the domestic state, fears vice (in the acquisition of property) and shares his food (with others)

pope: If love and virtue in the household reign, This is of life the perfect grace and gain
drewLazarus: If the married life possess love and virtue, these will be both its duty and reward

pope: If man in active household life a virtuous soul retain, What fruit from other modes of virtue can he gain
drewLazarus: What will he who lives virtuously in the domestic state gain by going into the other, (ascetic) state ?

pope: In nature's way who spends his calm domestic days,'Mid all that strive for virtue's crown hath foremost place
drewLazarus: Among all those who labour (for future happiness) he is greatest who lives well in the household state

pope: Others it sets upon their way, itself from virtue ne'er declines; Than stern ascetics' pains such life domestic brighter shines
drewLazarus: The householder who, not swerving from virtue, helps the ascetic in his way, endures more than those who endure penance

pope: The life domestic rightly bears true virtue's name; That other too, if blameless found, due praise may claim
drewLazarus: The marriage state is truly called virtue The other state is also good, if others do not reproach it

pope: Who shares domestic life, by household virtues graced, Shall, mid the Gods, in heaven who dwell, be placed
drewLazarus: He who on earth has lived in the conjugal state as he should live, will be placed among the Gods who dwell in heaven

pope: As doth the house beseem, she shows her wifely dignity; As doth her husband's wealth befit, she spends: help - meet is she
drewLazarus: She who has the excellence of home virtues, and can expend within the means of her husband, is a help in the domestic state

pope: If household excellence be wanting in the wife, Howe'er with splendour lived, all worthless is the life
drewLazarus: If the wife be devoid of domestic excellence, whatever (other) greatness be possessed, the conjugal state, is nothing

pope: There is no lack within the house, where wife in worth excels, There is no luck within the house, where wife dishonoured dwells
drewLazarus: If his wife be eminent (in virtue), what does (that man) not possess ? If she be without excellence, what does (he) possess ?

pope: If woman might of chastity retain, What choicer treasure doth the world contain
drewLazarus: What is more excellent than a wife, if she possess the stability of chastity ?

pope: No God adoring, low she bends before her lord; Then rising, serves: the rain falls instant at her word
drewLazarus: If she, who does not worship God, but who rising worships her husband, say, "let it rain," it will rain

pope: Who guards herself, for husband's comfort cares, her household's fame, In perfect wise with sleepless soul preserves, -give her a woman's name
drewLazarus: She is a wife who unweariedly guards herself, takes care of her husband, and preserves an unsullied fame

pope: Of what avail is watch and ward?Honour's woman's safest guard
drewLazarus: What avails the guard of a prison ? The chief guard of a woman is her chastity

pope: If wife be wholly true to him who gained her as his bride, Great glory gains she in the world where gods bliss abide
drewLazarus: If women shew reverence to their husbands, they will obtain great excellence in the world where the gods flourish

pope: Who have not spouses that in virtue's praise delight, They lion-like can never walk in scorner's sight
drewLazarus: The man whose wife seeks not the praise (of chastity) cannot walk with lion-like stately step, before those who revile them

pope: The house's 'blessing', men pronounce the house-wife excellent; The gain of blessed children is its goodly ornament
drewLazarus: The excellence of a wife is the good of her husband; and good children are the jewels of that goodness

pope: Of all that men acquire, we know not any greater gain, Than that which by the birth of learned children men obtain
drewLazarus: Among all the benefits that may be acquired, we know no greater benefit than the acquisition of intelligent children

pope: Who children gain, that none reproach, of virtuous worth, No evils touch them, through the sev'n-fold maze of birth
drewLazarus: The evils of the seven births shall not touch those who abtain children of a good disposition, free from vice

pope: 'Man's children are his fortune,' say the wise; From each one's deeds his varied fortunes rise
drewLazarus: Men will call their sons their wealth, because it flows to them through the deeds which they (sons) perform on their behalf

pope: Than God's ambrosia sweeter far the food before men laid, In which the little hands of children of their own have play'd
drewLazarus: The rice in which the little hand of their children has dabbled will be far sweeter (to the parent) than ambrosia

pope: To patent sweet the touch of children dear; Their voice is sweetest music to his ear
drewLazarus: The touch of children gives pleasure to the body, and the hearing of their words, pleasure to the ear

pope: 'The pipe is sweet,' 'the lute is sweet,' by them't will be averred, Who music of their infants' lisping lips have never heard
drewLazarus: "The pipe is sweet, the lute is sweet," say those who have not heard the prattle of their own children

pope: Sire greatest boon on son confers, who makes him meet, In councils of the wise to fill the highest seat
drewLazarus: The benefit which a father should confer on his son is to give him precedence in the assembly of the learned

pope: Their children's wisdom greater than their own confessed, Through the wide world is sweet to every human breast
drewLazarus: That their children should possess knowledge is more pleasing to all men of this great earth than to themselves

pope: When mother hears him named 'fulfill'd of wisdom's lore,'Far greater joy she feels, than when her son she bore
drewLazarus: The mother who hears her son called "a wise man" will rejoice more than she did at his birth

pope: To sire, what best requital can by grateful child be done?To make men say, 'What merit gained the father such a son?'
drewLazarus: (So to act) that it may be said "by what great penance did his father beget him," is the benefit which a son should render to his father

pope: And is there bar that can even love restrain?The tiny tear shall make the lover's secret plain
drewLazarus: Is there any fastening that can shut in love ? Tears of the affectionate will publish the love that is within

pope: The loveless to themselves belong alone; The loving men are others' to the very bone
drewLazarus: Those who are destitute of love appropriate all they have to themselves; but those who possess love consider even their bones to belong to others

pope: Of precious soul with body's flesh and bone, The union yields one fruit, the life of love alone
drewLazarus: They say that the union of soul and body in man is the fruit of the union of love and virtue (in a former birth)

pope: From love fond yearning springs for union sweet of minds; And that the bond of rare excelling friendship binds
drewLazarus: Love begets desire: and that (desire) begets the immeasureable excellence of friendship

pope: Sweetness on earth and rarest bliss above, These are the fruits of tranquil life of love
drewLazarus: These are the fruits of tranquil life of love

pope: The unwise deem love virtue only can sustain, It also helps the man who evil would restrain
drewLazarus: The ignorant say that love is an ally to virtue only, but it is also a help to get out of vice

pope: As sun's fierce ray dries up the boneless things, So loveless beings virtue's power to nothing brings
drewLazarus: Virtue will burn up the soul which is without love, even as the sun burns up the creature which is without bone, ie worms

pope: The loveless soul, the very joys of life may know, When flowers, in barren soil, on sapless trees, shall blow
drewLazarus: The domestic state of that man whose mind is without love is like the flourishing of a withered tree upon the parched desert

pope: Though every outward part complete, the body's fitly framed; What good, when soul within, of love devoid, lies halt and maimed
drewLazarus: Of what avail are all the external members (of the body) to those who are destitute of love, the internal member

pope: Bodies of loveless men are bony framework clad with skin; Then is the body seat of life, when love resides within
drewLazarus: That body alone which is inspired with love contains a living soul: if void of it, (the body) is bone overlaid with skin

pope: All household cares and course of daily life have this in viewGuests to receive with courtesy, and kindly acts to do
drewLazarus: The whole design of living in the domestic state and laying up (property) is (to be able) to exercise the benevolence of hospitality

pope: Though food of immortality should crown the board, Feasting alone, the guests without unfed, is thing abhorred
drewLazarus: It is not fit that one should wish his guests to be outside (his house) even though he were eating the food of immortality

pope: Each day he tends the coming guest with kindly care; Painless, unfailing plenty shall his household share
drewLazarus: The domestic life of the man that daily entertains the guests who come to him shall not be laid waste by poverty

pope: With smiling face he entertains each virtuous guest,'Fortune' with gladsome mind shall in his dwelling rest
drewLazarus: Lakshmi with joyous mind shall dwell in the house of that man who, with cheerful countenance, entertains the good as guests

pope: Who first regales his guest, and then himself supplies, O'er all his fields, unsown, shall plenteous harvests rise
drewLazarus: Is it necessary to sow the field of the man who, having feasted his guests, eats what may remain ?

pope: The guest arrived he tends, the coming guest expects to see; To those in heavenly homes that dwell a welcome guest is he
drewLazarus: He who, having entertained the guests that have come, looks out for others who may yet come, will be a welcome guest to the inhabitants of heaven

pope: To reckon up the fruit of kindly deeds were all in vain; Their worth is as the worth of guests you entertain
drewLazarus: The advantages of benevolence cannot be measured; the measure (of the virtue) of the guests (entertained) is the only measure

pope: With pain they guard their stores, yet 'All forlorn are we,' they'll cry, Who cherish not their guests, nor kindly help supply
drewLazarus: Those who have taken no part in the benevolence of hospitality shall (at length lament) saying, "we have laboured and laid up wealth and are now without support."

pope: To turn from guests is penury, though worldly goods abound;'Tis senseless folly, only with the senseless found
drewLazarus: That stupidity which excercises no hospitality is poverty in the midst of wealth It is the property of the stupid

pope: The flower of 'Anicha' withers away, If you do but its fragrance inhale; If the face of the host cold welcome convey, The guest's heart within him will fail
drewLazarus: As the Anicham flower fades in smelling, so fades the guest when the face is turned away

pope: Pleasant words are words with all pervading love that burn; Words from his guileless mouth who can the very truth discern
drewLazarus: Sweet words are those which imbued with love and free from deceit flow from the mouth of the virtuous

pope: A pleasant word with beaming smile's preferred, Even to gifts with liberal heart conferred
drewLazarus: Sweet speech, with a cheerful countenance is better than a gift made with a joyous mind

pope: With brightly beaming smile, and kindly light of loving eye, And heart sincere, to utter pleasant words is charity
drewLazarus: Sweet speech, flowing from the heart (uttered) with a cheerful countenance and a sweet look, is true virtue

pope: The men of pleasant speech that gladness breathe around, Through indigence shall never sorrow's prey be found
drewLazarus: Sorrow-increasing poverty shall not come upon those who use towards all, pleasure-increasing sweetness of speech

pope: Humility with pleasant speech to man on earth, Is choice adornment; all besides is nothing worth
drewLazarus: Humility and sweetness of speech are the ornaments of man; all others are not (ornaments)

pope: Who seeks out good, words from his lips of sweetness flow; In him the power of vice declines, and virtues grow
drewLazarus: If a man, while seeking to speak usefully, speaks also sweetly, his sins will diminish and his virtue increase

pope: The words of sterling sense, to rule of right that strict adhere, To virtuous action prompting, blessings yield in every sphere
drewLazarus: That speech which, while imparting benefits ceases not to please, will yield righteousness (for this world) and merit (for the next world)

pope: Sweet kindly words, from meanness free, delight of heart, In world to come and in this world impart
drewLazarus: Sweet speech, free from harm to others, will give pleasure both in this world and in the next

pope: Who sees the pleasure kindly speech affords, Why makes he use of harsh, repellant words
drewLazarus: Why does he use harsh words, who sees the pleasure which sweet speech yields ?

pope: When pleasant words are easy, bitter words to use, Is, leaving sweet ripe fruit, the sour unripe to choose
drewLazarus: To say disagreeable things when agreeable are at hand is like eating unripe fruit when there is ripe

pope: Assistance given by those who ne'er received our aid, Is debt by gift of heaven and earth but poorly paid
drewLazarus: (The gift of) heaven and earth is not an equivalent for a benefit which is conferred where none had been received

pope: A timely benefit, -though thing of little worth, The gift itself, -in excellence transcends the earth
drewLazarus: A favour conferred in the time of need, though it be small (in itself), is (in value) much larger than the world

pope: Kindness shown by those who weigh not what the return may be:When you ponder right its merit, 'Tis vaster than the sea
drewLazarus: If we weigh the excellence of a benefit which is conferred without weighing the return, it is larger than the sea

pope: Each benefit to those of actions' fruit who rightly deem, Though small as millet-seed, as palm-tree vast will seem
drewLazarus: Though the benefit conferred be as small as a millet seed, those who know its advantage will consider it as large as a palmyra fruit

pope: The kindly aid's extent is of its worth no measure true; Its worth is as the worth of him to whom the act you do
drewLazarus: The benefit itself is not the measure of the benefit; the worth of those who have received it is its measure

pope: Kindness of men of stainless soul remember evermoreForsake thou never friends who were thy stay in sorrow sore
drewLazarus: Forsake not the friendship of those who have been your staff in adversity Forget not be benevolence of the blameless

pope: Through all seven worlds, in seven-fold birth, Remains in mem'ry of the wiseFriendship of those who wiped on earth, The tears of sorrow from their eyes
drewLazarus: (The wise) will remember throughout their seven-fold births the love of those who have wiped away their affliction

pope: 'Tis never good to let the thought of good things done thee pass away; Of things not good, 'tis good to rid thy memory that very day
drewLazarus: It is not good to forget a benefit; it is good to forget an injury even in the very moment (in which it is inflicted)

pope: Effaced straightway is deadliest injury, By thought of one kind act in days gone by
drewLazarus: Though one inflict an injury great as murder, it will perish before the thought of one benefit (formerly) conferred

pope: Who every good have killed, may yet destruction flee; Who 'benefit' has killed, that man shall ne'er 'scape free
drewLazarus: He who has killed every virtue may yet escape; there is no escape for him who has killed a benefit

pope: If justice, failing not, its quality maintain, Giving to each his due, -'tis man's one highest gain
drewLazarus: That equity which consists in acting with equal regard to each of (the three) divisions of men [enemies, strangers and friends] is a pre-eminent virtue

pope: The just man's wealth unwasting shall endure, And to his race a lasting joy ensure
drewLazarus: The wealth of the man of rectitude will not perish, but will bring happiness also to his posterity

pope: Though only good it seem to give, yet gainBy wrong acquired, not e'en one day retain
drewLazarus: Forsake in the very moment (of acquisition) that gain which, though it should bring advantage, is without equity

pope: Who just or unjust lived shall soon appear:By each one's offspring shall the truth be clear
drewLazarus: The worthy and unworthy may be known by the existence or otherwise of good offsprings

pope: The gain and loss in life are not mere accident; Just mind inflexible is sages' ornament
drewLazarus: Loss and gain come not without cause; it is the ornament of the wise to preserve evenness of mind (under both)

pope: If, right deserting, heart to evil turn, Let man impending ruin's sign discern
drewLazarus: Let him whose mind departing from equity commits sin well consider thus within himself, "I shall perish."

pope: The man who justly lives, tenacious of the right, In low estate is never low to wise man's sight
drewLazarus: The great will not regard as poverty the low estate of that man who dwells in the virtue of equity

pope: To stand, like balance-rod that level hangs and rightly weighs, With calm unbiassed equity of soul, is sages' praise
drewLazarus: To incline to neither side, but to rest impartial as the even-fixed scale is the ornament of the wise

pope: Inflexibility in word is righteousness, If men inflexibility of soul possess
drewLazarus: Freedom from obliquity of speech is rectitude, if there be (corresponding) freedom from bias of mind

pope: As thriving trader is the trader known, Who guards another's interests as his own
drewLazarus: The true merchandize of merchants is to guard and do by the things of others as they do by their own

pope: Control of self does man conduct to bliss th' immortals share; Indulgence leads to deepest night, and leaves him there
drewLazarus: Self-control will place (a man) among the Gods; the want of it will drive (him) into the thickest darkness (of hell)

pope: Guard thou as wealth the power of self-control; Than this no greater gain to living soul
drewLazarus: Let self-control be guarded as a treasure; there is no greater source of good for man than that

pope: If versed in wisdom's lore by virtue's law you self restrainYour self-repression known will yield you glory's gain
drewLazarus: Knowing that self-control is knowledge, if a man should control himself, in the prescribed course, such self-control will bring him distinction among the wise

pope: In his station, all unswerving, if man self subdue, Greater he than mountain proudly rising to the view
drewLazarus: More lofty than a mountain will be the greatness of that man who without swerving from his domestic state, controls himself

pope: To all humility is goodly grace; but chief to themWith fortune blessed, -'tis fortune's diadem
drewLazarus: Humility is good in all; but especially in the rich it is (the excellence of) higher riches

pope: Like tortoise, who the five restrainsIn one, through seven world bliss obtains
drewLazarus: Should one throughout a single birth, like a tortoise keep in his five senses, the fruit of it will prove a safe-guard to him throughout the seven-fold births.

pope: Whate'er they fail to guard, o'er lips men guard should keep; If not, through fault of tongue, they bitter tears shall weep
drewLazarus: Whatever besides you leave unguarded, guard your tongue; otherwise errors of speech and the consequent misery will ensue

pope: Though some small gain of good it seem to bring, The evil word is parent still of evil thing
drewLazarus: If a man's speech be productive of a single evil, all the good by him will be turned into evil

pope: In flesh by fire inflamed, nature may thoroughly heal the sore; In soul by tongue inflamed, the ulcer healeth never more
drewLazarus: The wound which has been burnt in by fire may heal, but a wound burnt in by the tongue will never heal

pope: Who learns restraint, and guards his soul from wrath, Virtue, a timely aid, attends his path
drewLazarus: Virtue, seeking for an opportunity, will come into the path of that man who, possessed of learning and self-control, guards himself against anger

pope: 'Decorum' gives especial excellence; with greater care'Decorum' should men guard than life, which all men share
drewLazarus: Propriety of conduct leads to eminence, it should therefore be preserved more carefully than life

pope: Searching, duly watching, learning, 'decorum' still we find; Man's only aid; toiling, guard thou this with watchful mind
drewLazarus: Let propriety of conduct be laboriously preserved and guarded; though one know and practise and excel in many virtues, that will be an eminent aid

pope: 'Decorum's' true nobility on earth;'Indecorum's' issue is ignoble birth
drewLazarus: Propriety of conduct is true greatness of birth, and impropriety will sink into a mean birth

pope: Though he forget, the Brahman may regain his Vedic lore; Failing in 'decorum due,' birthright's gone for evermore
drewLazarus: A Brahman though he should forget the Vedas may recover it by reading; but, if he fail in propriety of conduct even his high birth will be destroyed

pope: The envious soul in life no rich increase of blessing gains, So man of 'due decorum' void no dignity obtains
drewLazarus: Just as the envious man will be without wealth, so will the man of destitute of propriety of conduct be without greatness

pope: The strong of soul no jot abate of 'strict decorum's' laws, Knowing that 'due decorum's' breach foulest disgrace will cause
drewLazarus: Those firm in mind will not slacken in their observance of the proprieties of life, knowing, as they do, the misery that flows from the transgression from them

pope: 'Tis source of dignity when 'true decorum' is preserved; Who break 'decorum's' rules endure e'en censures undeserved
drewLazarus: From propriety of conduct men obtain greatness; from impropriety comes insufferable disgrace

pope: 'Decorum true' observed a seed of good will be;'Decorum's breach' will sorrow yield eternally
drewLazarus: Propriety of conduct is the seed of virtue; impropriety will ever cause sorrow

pope: It cannot be that they who 'strict decorum's' law fulfil, E'en in forgetful mood, should utter words of ill
drewLazarus: Those who study propriety of conduct will not speak evil, even forgetfully

pope: Who know not with the world in harmony to dwell, May many things have learned, but nothing well
drewLazarus: Those who know not how to act agreeably to the world, though they have learnt many things, are still ignorant

pope: Who laws of virtue and possession's rights have known, Indulge no foolish love of her by right another's own
drewLazarus: The folly of desiring her who is the property of another will not be found in those who know (the attributes of) virtue and (the rights of) property

pope: No fools, of all that stand from virtue's pale shut out, Like those who longing lurk their neighbour's gate without
drewLazarus: Among all those who stand on the outside of virtue, there are no greater fools than those who stand outside their neighbour's door

pope: They're numbered with the dead, e'en while they live, -how otherwise?With wife of sure confiding friend who evil things devise
drewLazarus: Certainly they are no better than dead men who desire evil towards the wife of those who

pope: How great soe'er they be, what gain have they of life, Who, not a whit reflecting, seek a neighbour's wife
drewLazarus: However great one may be, what does it avail if, without at all considering his guilt, he goes unto the wife of another ?

pope: 'Mere triflel' saying thus, invades the home, so he ensuresA gain of guilt that deathless aye endures
drewLazarus: He who thinks lightly of going into the wife of another acquires guilt that will abide with him imperishably and for ever

pope: Who home ivades, from him pass nevermore, Hatred and sin, fear, foul disgrace; these four
drewLazarus: Hatred, sin, fear, disgrace; these four will never leave him who goes in to his neighbour's wife

pope: Who sees the wife, another's own, with no desiring eyeIn sure domestic bliss he dwelleth ever virtuously
drewLazarus: He who desires not the womanhood of her who should walk according to the will of another will be praised as a virtuous house-holder

pope: Manly excellence, that looks not on another's wife, Is not virtue merely, 'tis full 'propriety' of life
drewLazarus: That noble manliness which looks not at the wife of another is the virtue and dignity of the great

pope: Who 're good indeed, on earth begirt by ocean's gruesome tide?The men who touch not her that is another's bride
drewLazarus: Is it asked, "who are those who shall obtain good in this world surrounded by the terror-producing sea ?" Those who touch not the shoulder of her who belongs to another

pope: Though virtue's bounds he pass, and evil deeds hath wrought; At least, 'tis good if neighbour's wife he covet not
drewLazarus: Though a man perform no virtuous deeds and commit (every) vice, it will be well if he desire not the womanhood of her who is within the limit (of the house) of another

pope: As earth bears up the men who delve into her breast, To bear with scornful men of virtues is the best
drewLazarus: To bear with those who revile us, just as the earth bears up those who dig it, is the first of virtues

pope: Forgiving trespasses is good always; Forgetting them hath even higher praise;
drewLazarus: Bear with reproach even when you can retaliate; but to forget it will be still better than that

pope: The sorest poverty is bidding guest unfed depart; The mightiest might to bear with men of foolish heart
drewLazarus: To neglect hospitality is poverty of poverty To bear with the ignorant is might of might

pope: Seek'st thou honour never tarnished to retain; So must thou patience, guarding evermore, maintain
drewLazarus: If you desire that greatness should never leave, you preserve in your conduct the exercise of patience

pope: Who wreak their wrath as worthless are despised; Who patiently forbear as gold are prized
drewLazarus: (The wise) will not at all esteem the resentful They will esteem the patient just as the gold which they lay up with care

pope: Who wreak their wrath have pleasure for a day; Who bear have praise till earth shall pass away
drewLazarus: The pleasure of the resentful continues for a day The praise of the patient will continue until (the final destruction of) the world

pope: Though others work thee ill, thus shalt thou blessing reap; Grieve for their sin, thyself from vicious action keep
drewLazarus: Though others inflict injuries on you, yet compassionating the evil (that will come upon them) it will be well not to do them anything contrary to virtue

pope: With overweening pride when men with injuries assail, By thine own righteous dealing shalt thou mightily prevail
drewLazarus: Let a man by patience overcome those who through pride commit excesses

pope: They who transgressors' evil words endureWith patience, are as stern ascetics pure
drewLazarus: Those who bear with the uncourteous speech of the insolent are as pure as the ascetics

pope: Though 'great' we deem the men that fast and suffer pain, Who others' bitter words endure, the foremost place obtain
drewLazarus: Those who endure abstinence from food are great, next to those who endure the uncourteous speech of others

pope: As 'strict decorum's' laws, that all men bind, Let each regard unenvying grace of mind
drewLazarus: Let a man esteem that disposition which is free from envy in the same manner as propriety of conduct

pope: If man can learn to envy none on earth,'Tis richest gift, -beyond compare its worth
drewLazarus: Amongst all attainable excellences there is none equal to that of being free from envy towords others

pope: Nor wealth nor virtue does that man desire 'tis plain, Whom others' wealth delights not, feeling envious pain
drewLazarus: Of him who instead of rejoicing in the wealth of others, envies it, it will be said "he neither desires virtue not wealth."

pope: The wise through envy break not virtue's laws, Knowing ill-deeds of foul disgrace the cause
drewLazarus: (The wise) knowing the misery that comes from transgression will not through envy commit unrighteous deeds

pope: Envy they have within! Enough to seat their fate!Though foemen fail, envy can ruin consummate
drewLazarus: To those who cherish envy that is enough Though free from enemies that (envy) will bring destruction

pope: Who scans good gifts to others given with envious eye, His kin, with none to clothe or feed them, surely die
drewLazarus: He who is envious at a gift (made to another) will with his relations utterly perish destitute of food and rainment

pope: From envious man good fortune's goddess turns away, Grudging him good, and points him out misfortune's prey
drewLazarus: Lakshmi envying (the prosperity) of the envious man will depart and introduce him to her sister

pope: Envy, embodied ill, incomparable bane, Good fortune slays, and soul consigns to fiery pain
drewLazarus: Envy will destroy (a man's) wealth (in his world) and drive him into the pit of fire (in the world to come.)

pope: To men of envious heart, when comes increase of joy, Or loss to blameless men, the 'why' will thoughtful hearts employ
drewLazarus: The wealth of a man of envious mind and the poverty of the righteous will be pondered

pope: No envious men to large and full felicity attain; No men from envy free have failed a sure increase to gain
drewLazarus: Never have the envious become great; never have those who are free from envy been without greatness

pope: With soul unjust to covet others' well-earned store, Brings ruin to the home, to evil opes the door
drewLazarus: If a man departing from equity covet the property (of others), at that very time will his family be destroyed and guilt be incurred

pope: Through lust of gain, no deeds that retribution bring, Do they, who shrink with shame from every unjust thing
drewLazarus: Those who blush at the want of equity will not commit disgraceful acts through desire of the profit that may be gained

pope: No deeds of ill, misled by base desire, Do they, whose souls to other joys aspire
drewLazarus: Those who desire the higher pleasures (of heaven) will not act unjustly through desire of the trifling joy. (in this life.)

pope: Men who have conquered sense, with sight from sordid vision freed, Desire not other's goods, e'en in the hour of sorest need
drewLazarus: The wise who have conquered their senses and are free from crime, will not covet (the things of others), with the thought "we are destitute."

pope: What gain, though lore refined of amplest reach he learn, His acts towards all mankind if covetous desire to folly turn
drewLazarus: What is the advantage of extensive and accurate knowledge if a man through covetousness act senselessly towards all ?

pope: Though, grace desiring, he in virtue's way stand strong, He's lost who wealth desires, and ponders deeds of wrong
drewLazarus: If he, who through desire of the virtue of kindness abides in the domestic state ie, the path in which it may be obtained, covet (the property of others) and think of evil methods (to obtain it), he will perish

pope: Seek not increase by greed of gain acquired; That fruit matured yields never good desired
drewLazarus: Desire not the gain of covetousness In the enjoyment of its fruits there is no glory

pope: What saves prosperity from swift decline?Absence of lust to make another's cherished riches thine
drewLazarus: If it is weighed, "what is the indestructibility of wealth," it is freedom from covetousness

pope: Good fortune draws anigh in helpful time of need, To him who, schooled in virtue, guards his soul from greed
drewLazarus: Lakshmi, knowing the manner (in which she may approach) will immediately come to those wise men who, knowing that it is virtue, covet not the property of others

pope: From thoughtless lust of other's goods springs fatal ill, Greatness of soul that covets not shall triumph still
drewLazarus: To covet (the wealth of another) regardless of consequences will bring destruction That greatness (of mind) which covets not will give victory

pope: Though virtuous words his lips speak not, and all his deeds are illIf neighbour he defame not, there's good within him still
drewLazarus: Though one do not even speak of virtue and live in sin, it will be well if it be said of him "he does not backbite."

pope: Than he who virtue scorns, and evil deeds performs, more vile, Is he that slanders friend, then meets him with false smile
drewLazarus: To smile deceitfully (in another's presence) after having reviled him to his destruction (behind his back) is a greater evil than the commission of (every other) sin and the destruction of (every) virtue

pope: 'Tis greater gain of virtuous good for man to die, Than live to slander absent friend, and falsely praise when nigh
drewLazarus: Death rather than life will confer upon the deceitful backbiter the profit which (the treatises on) virtue point out

pope: In presence though unkindly words you speak, say notIn absence words whose ill result exceeds your thought
drewLazarus: Though you speak without kindness before another's face speak not in his absence words which regard not the evil subsequently resulting from it

pope: The slanderous meanness that an absent friend defames,'This man in words owns virtue, not in heart,' proclaims
drewLazarus: The emptiness of that man's mind who (merely) praises virtue will be seen from the meanness of reviling another behind his back

pope: Who on his neighbours' sins delights to dwell, The story of his sins, culled out with care, the world will tell
drewLazarus: The character of the faults of that man who publishes abroad the faults of others will be sought out and published

pope: With friendly art who know not pleasant words to say, Speak words that sever hearts, and drive choice friends away
drewLazarus: Those who know not to live in friendship with amusing conversation will by back-biting estrange even their relatives

pope: Whose nature bids them faults of closest friends proclaimWhat mercy will they show to other men's good name
drewLazarus: What will those not do to strangers whose nature leads them to publish abroad the faults of their intimate friends ?

pope: 'Tis charity, I ween, that makes the earth sustain their loadWho, neighbours' absence watching, tales or slander tell abroad
drewLazarus: The world through charity supports the weight of those who reproach others observing their absence

pope: If each his own, as neighbours' faults would scan, Could any evil hap to living man
drewLazarus: If they observed their own faults as they observe the faults of others, would any evil happen to men ?

pope: Words without sense, while chafe the wise, Who babbles, him will all despise
drewLazarus: He who to the disgust of many speaks useless things will be despised by all

pope: Words without sense, where many wise men hear, to pourThan deeds to friends ungracious done offendeth more
drewLazarus: To speak useless things in the presence of many is a greater evil than to do unkind things towards friends

pope: Diffusive speech of useless words proclaimsA man who never righteous wisdom gains
drewLazarus: That conversation in which a man utters forth useless things will say of him "he is without virtue."

pope: Unmeaning, worthless words, said to the multitude, To none delight afford, and sever men from good
drewLazarus: The words devoid of profit or pleasure which a man speaks will, being inconsistent with virtue,

pope: Gone are both fame and boasted excellence, When men of worth speak of words devoid of sense
drewLazarus: If the good speak vain words their eminence and excellence will leave them

pope: Who makes display of idle words' inanity, Call him not man, -chaff of humanity
drewLazarus: Call not him a man who parades forth his empty words Call him the chaff of men

pope: Let those who list speak things that no delight afford,'Tis good for men of worth to speak no idle word
drewLazarus: Let the wise if they will, speak things without excellence; it will be well for them not to speak useless things

pope: The wise who weigh the worth of every utterance, Speak none but words of deep significance
drewLazarus: The wise who seek after rare pleasures will not speak words that have not much weight in them

pope: The men of vision pure, from wildering folly free, Not e'en in thoughtless hour, speak words of vanity
drewLazarus: Those wise men who are without faults and are freed from ignorance will not even forgetfully speak things that profit not

pope: If speak you will, speak words that fruit afford, If speak you will, speak never fruitless word
drewLazarus: Speak what is useful, and speak not useless words

pope: With sinful act men cease to feel the dread of ill within, The excellent will dread the wanton pride of cherished sin
drewLazarus: Those who have experience of evil deeds will not fear, but the excellent will fear the pride of sin

pope: Since evils new from evils ever grow, Evil than fire works out more dreaded woe
drewLazarus: Because evil produces evil, therefore should evil be feared more than fire

pope: Even to those that hate make no return of ill; So shalt thou wisdom's highest law, 'tis said, fulfil
drewLazarus: So shalt thou wisdom's highest law, 'tis said, fulfil

pope: Though good thy soul forget, plot not thy neighbour's fall, Thy plans shall 'virtue's Power' by ruin to thyself forestall
drewLazarus: Even though forgetfulness meditate not the ruin of another Virtue will meditate the ruin of him who thus meditates

pope: Make not thy poverty a plea for ill; Thy evil deeds will make thee poorer still
drewLazarus: Commit not evil, saying, "I am poor": if you do, you will become poorer still

pope: What ranks as evil spare to do, if thou would'st shunAffliction sore through ill to thee by others done
drewLazarus: Let him not do evil to others who desires not that sorrows should pursue him

pope: From every enmity incurred there is to 'scape, a way; The wrath of evil deeds will dog men's steps, and slay
drewLazarus: However great be the enmity men have incurred they may still live The enmity of sin will incessantly pursue and kill

pope: Man's shadow dogs his steps where'er he wends; Destruction thus on sinful deeds attends
drewLazarus: Destruction will dwell at the heels of those who commit evil even as their shadow that leaves them not

pope: Beware, if to thyself thyself is dear, Lest thou to aught that ranks as ill draw near
drewLazarus: If a man love himself, let him not commit any sin however small

pope: The man, to devious way of sin that never turned aside, From ruin rests secure, whatever ills betide
drewLazarus: Know ye that he is freed from destruction who commits no evil, going to neither side of the right path

pope: Duty demands no recompense; to clouds of heaven, By men on earth, what answering gift is given
drewLazarus: Benevolence seeks not a return. What does the world give back to the clouds ?

pope: The worthy say, when wealth rewards their toil-spent hours, For uses of beneficence alone 'tis ours
drewLazarus: All the wealth acquired with perseverance by the worthy is for the exercise of benevolence

pope: To 'due beneficence' no equal good we know, Amid the happy gods, or in this world below
drewLazarus: It is difficult to obtain another good equal to benevolence either in this world or in that of the gods

pope: Who knows what's human life's befitting grace, He lives; the rest 'mongst dead men have their place
drewLazarus: He truly lives who knows (and discharges) the proper duties (of benevolence) He who knows them not will be reckoned among the dead

pope: The wealth of men who love the 'fitting way,' the truly wise, Is as when water fills the lake that village needs supplies
drewLazarus: The wealth of that man of eminent knowledge who desires to exercise the benevolence approved of by the world, is like the full waters of a city-tank

pope: A tree that fruits in th' hamlet's central mart, Is wealth that falls to men of liberal heart
drewLazarus: The wealth of a man (possessed of the virtue) of benevolence is like the ripening of a fruitful tree in the midst of a town

pope: Unfailing tree that healing balm distils from every part, Is ample wealth that falls to him of large and noble heart
drewLazarus: If wealth be in the possession of a man who has the great excellence (of benevolence), it is like a tree which as a medicine is an infallible cure for disease

pope: E'en when resources fall, they weary not of 'kindness due,'-They to whom Duty's self appears in vision true
drewLazarus: The wise who know what is duty will not scant their benevolence even when they are without wealth

pope: The kindly-hearted man is poor in this alone, When power of doing deeds of goodness he finds none
drewLazarus: The poverty of a benevolent man, is nothing but his inability to exercise the same

pope: Though by 'beneficence,' the loss of all should come,'Twere meet man sold himself, and bought it with the sum
drewLazarus: If it be said that loss will result from benevolence, such loss is worth being procured even by the sale of one's self

pope: Call that a gift to needy men thou dost dispense, All else is void of good, seeking for recompense
drewLazarus: To give to the destitute is true charity All other gifts have the nature of (what is done for) a measured return

pope: Though men declare it heavenward path, yet to receive is ill; Though upper heaven were not, to give is virtue still
drewLazarus: To beg is evil, even though it were said that it is a good path (to heaven) To give is good, even though it were said that those who do so cannot obtain heaven

pope: 'I've nought' is ne'er the high-born man's reply; He gives to those who raise themselves that cry
drewLazarus: (Even in a low state) not to adopt the mean expedient of saying "I have nothing," but to give, is the characteristic of the mad of noble birth

pope: The suppliants' cry for aid yields scant delight, Until you see his face with grateful gladness bright
drewLazarus: To see men begging from us in disagreeable, until we see their pleasant countenance

pope: 'Mid devotees they're great who hunger's pangs sustain, Who hunger's pangs relieve a higher merit gain
drewLazarus: The power of those who perform penance is the power of enduring hunger It is inferior to the power of those who remove the hunger (of others)

pope: Let man relieve the wasting hunger men endure; For treasure gained thus finds he treasure-house secure
drewLazarus: The removal of the killing hunger of the poor is the place for one to lay up his wealth

pope: Whose soul delights with hungry men to share his meal, The hand of hunger's sickness sore shall never feel
drewLazarus: The fiery disease of hunger shall never touch him who habitually distributes his food to others

pope: Delight of glad'ning human hearts with gifts do they not know.Men of unpitying eye, who hoard their wealth and lose it so
drewLazarus: Do the hard-eyed who lay up and lose their possessions not know the happiness which springs from the pleasure of giving ?

pope: They keep their garners full, for self alone the board they spread;-'Tis greater pain, be sure, than begging daily bread
drewLazarus: Solitary and unshared eating for the sake of filling up one's own riches is certainly much more

pope: 'Tis bitter pain to die, 'Tis worse to live.For him who nothing finds to give
drewLazarus: Nothing is more unpleasant than death: yet even that is pleasant where charity cannot be exercised

pope: See that thy life the praise of generous gifts obtain; Save this for living man exists no real gain
drewLazarus: Give to the poor and live with praise There is no greater profit to man than that

pope: The speech of all that speak agrees to crownThe men that give to those that ask, with fair renown
drewLazarus: Whatsoever is spoken in the world will abide as praise upon that man who gives alms to the poor

pope: Save praise alone that soars on high, Nought lives on earth that shall not die
drewLazarus: There is nothing that stands forth in the world imperishable, except fame, exalted in solitary greatness

pope: If men do virtuous deeds by world-wide ample glory crowned, The heavens will cease to laud the sage for other gifts renowned
drewLazarus: If one has acquired extensive fame within the limits of this earth, the world of the Gods will no longer praise those sages who have attained that world

pope: Loss that is gain, and death of life's true bliss fulfilled, Are fruits which only wisdom rare can yield
drewLazarus: Prosperity to the body of fame, resulting in poverty to the body of flesh and the stability to the former arising from the death of the latter, are achievable only by the wise

pope: If man you walk the stage, appear adorned with glory's grace; Save glorious you can shine, 'twere better hide your face
drewLazarus: If you are born (in this world), be born with qualities conductive to fame From those who are destitute of them it will be better not to be born

pope: If you your days will spend devoid of goodly fame, When men despise, why blame them? You've yourself to blame
drewLazarus: Why do those who cannot live with praise, grieve those who despise them, instead of grieving themselves for their own inability

pope: Fame is virtue's child, they say; if, then, You childless live, you live the scorn of men
drewLazarus: Not to beget fame will be esteemed a disgrace by the wise in this world

pope: The blameless fruits of fields' increase will dwindle down, If earth the burthen bear of men without renown
drewLazarus: The ground which supports a body without fame will diminish in its rich produce

pope: Who live without reproach, them living men we deem; Who live without renown, live not, though living men they seem
drewLazarus: Those live who live without disgrace Those who live without fame live not

pope: Wealth 'mid wealth is wealth 'kindliness'; Wealth of goods the vilest too possess
drewLazarus: The wealth of kindness is wealth of wealth, in as much as the wealth of property is possessed by the basest of men

pope: The law of 'grace' fulfil, by methods good due trial made, Though many systems you explore, this is your only aid
drewLazarus: (Stand) in the good path, consider, and be kind. Even considering according to the conflicting tenets of the different sects, kindness will be your best aid, (in the acquisition of heavenly bliss.)

pope: They in whose breast a 'gracious kindliness' resides, See not the gruesome world, where darkness drear abides
drewLazarus: They will never enter the world of darkness and wretchedness whose minds are the abode of kindness

pope: Who for undying souls of men provides with gracious zeal, In his own soul the dreaded guilt of sin shall never feel
drewLazarus: (The wise) say that the evils, which his soul would dread, will never come upon the man who exercises kindness and protects the life (of other creatures)

pope: The teeming earth's vast realm, round which the wild winds blow, Is witness, men of 'grace' no woeful want shall know
drewLazarus: This great rich earth over which the wind blows, is a witness that sorrow never comes upon the kindhearted

pope: Gain of true wealth oblivious they eschew, Who 'grace' forsake, and graceless actions do
drewLazarus: (The wise) say that those who neglect kindness and practise cruelties, neglected virtue (in their former birth), and forgot (the sorrows which they must suffer.)

pope: As to impoverished men this present world is not; The 'graceless' in you world have neither part nor lot
drewLazarus: As this world is not for those who are without wealth, so that world is not for those who are without kindness

pope: Who lose the flower of wealth, when seasons change, again may bloom; Who lose 'benevolence', lose all; nothing can change their doom
drewLazarus: Those who are without wealth may, at some future time, become prosperous; those who are destitute of kindness are utterly destitute; for them there is no change

pope: When souls unwise true wisdom's mystic vision see, The 'graceless' man may work true works of charity
drewLazarus: If you consider, the virtue of him who is without kindness is like the perception of the true being by him who is without wisdom

pope: When weaker men you front with threat'ning brow, Think how you felt in presence of some stronger foe
drewLazarus: When a man is about to rush upon those who are weaker than himself, let him remember how he has stood (trembling) before those who are stronger than himself

pope: How can the wont of 'kindly grace' to him be known, Who other creatures' flesh consumes to feed his own
drewLazarus: How can he be possessed of kindness, who to increase his own flesh, eats the flesh of other creatures

pope: No use of wealth have they who guard not their estate; No use of grace have they with flesh who hunger sate
drewLazarus: As those possess no property who do not take care of it, so those possess no kindness who feed on flesh

pope: Like heart of them that murderous weapons bear, his mind, Who eats of savoury meat, no joy in good can find
drewLazarus: Like the (murderous) mind of him who carries a weapon (in his hand), the mind of him who feasts with pleasure on the body of another (creature), has no regard for goodness

pope: 'What's grace, or lack of grace'? 'To kill' is this, that 'not to kill'; To eat dead flesh can never worthy end fulfil
drewLazarus: If it be asked what is kindness and what its opposite, the answer would be preservation and destruction of life; and therefore it is not right to feed on the flesh (obtained by taking away life)

pope: If flesh you eat not, life's abodes unharmed remain; Who eats, hell swallows him, and renders not again
drewLazarus: Not to eat flesh contributes to the continuance of life; therefore if a man eat flesh, hell will not open its mouth (to let him escape out, after he has once fallen in)

pope: 'We eat the slain,' you say, by us no living creatures die; Who'd kill and sell, I pray, if none came there the flesh to buy
drewLazarus: If the world does not destroy life for the purpose of eating, then no one would sell flesh for the sake of money

pope: With other beings' ulcerous wounds their hunger they appease; If this they felt, desire to eat must surely cease
drewLazarus: If men should come to know that flesh is nothing but the unclean ulcer of a body, let them abstain from eating it

pope: Whose souls the vision pure and passionless perceive, Eat not the bodies men of life bereave
drewLazarus: The wise, who have freed themselves from mental delusion, will not eat the flesh which has been severed from an animal

pope: Than thousand rich oblations, with libations rare, Better the flesh of slaughtered beings not to share
drewLazarus: Not to kill and eat (the flesh of) an animal, is better than the pouring forth of ghee etc, in a thousand sacrifices

pope: Who slays nought,- flesh rejects- his feet beforeAll living things with clasped hands adore
drewLazarus: All creatures will join their hands together, and worship him who has never taken away life, nor eaten flesh

pope: To bear due penitential pains, while no offenceHe causes others, is the type of 'penitence'
drewLazarus: The nature of religious discipline consists, in the endurance (by the ascetic) of the sufferings which it brings on himself, and in abstaining from giving pain to others

pope: To 'penitents' sincere avails their 'penitence'; Where that is not, 'tis but a vain pretence
drewLazarus: Austerities can only be borne, and their benefits enjoyed, by those who have practised them (in a former birth); it will be useless for those who have not done so, to attempt to practise them (now)

pope: Have other men forgotten 'penitence' who striveTo earn for penitents the things by which they live
drewLazarus: It is to provide food etc, for the ascetics who have abandoned (the desire of earthly possessions) that other persons have forgotten (to practise) austerity ?

pope: Destruction to his foes, to friends increase of joyThe 'penitent' can cause, if this his thoughts employ
drewLazarus: If (the ascetic) desire the destruction of his enemies, or the aggrandizement of his friends, it will be effected by (the power of) his austerities

pope: That what they wish may, as they wish, be won, By men on earth are works of painful 'penance' done
drewLazarus: Religious dislipline is practised in this world, because it secures the attainment of whatever one may wish to enjoy (in the world to come)

pope: Who works of 'penance' do, their end attain, Others in passion's net enshared, toil but in vain
drewLazarus: Those discharge their duty who perform austerities; all others accomplish their own destruction, through the entanglement of the desire (of riches and sensual pleasure)

pope: The hotter glows the fining fire, the gold the brighter shines; The pain of penitence, like fire, the soul of man refines
drewLazarus: Just as gold is purified as heated in the fire, will those shine, who have endured the burning of pain (in frequent austerities)

pope: Who gains himself in utter self-control, Him worships every other living soul
drewLazarus: All other creatures will worship him who has attained the control of his own soul

pope: E'en over death the victory he may gain, If power by penance won his soul obtain
drewLazarus: Those who have attained the power which religious discipline confers, will be able also to pass the limit of Yama, (the God of death)

pope: The many all things lack! The cause is plain, The 'penitents' are few The many shun such pain
drewLazarus: Because there are few who practise austerity and many who do not, there are many destitute and few rich in this world

pope: Who with deceitful mind in false way walks of covert sin, The five-fold elements his frame compose, decide within
drewLazarus: The five elements (of his body) will laugh within him at the feigned conduct of the deceitful minded man

pope: What gain, though virtue's semblance high as heaven his fame exalt, If heart dies down through sense of self-detected fault
drewLazarus: What avails an appearance (of sanctity) high as heaven, if his mind suffers (the indulgence) of conscious sin

pope: As if a steer should graze wrapped round with tiger's skin, Is show of virtuous might when weakness lurks within
drewLazarus: The assumed appearance of power, by a man who has no power (to restrain his senses and perform austerity), is like a cow feeding on grass covered with a tiger's skin

pope: 'Tis as a fowler, silly birds to snare, in thicket lurksWhen, clad in stern ascetic garb, one secret evil works
drewLazarus: He who hides himself under the mask of an ascetic and commits sins, like a sportsman who conceals himself in the thicket to catch birds

pope: 'Our souls are free,' who say, yet practise evil secretly,'What folly have we wrought!' by many shames o'er-whelmed, shall cry
drewLazarus: The false conduct of those who say they have renounced all desire will one day bring them sorrows that will make them cry out, "Oh! what have we done, what have we done."

pope: In mind renouncing nought, in speech renouncing every tie, Who guileful live,- no men are found than these of 'harder eye'
drewLazarus: Amongst living men there are none so hard-hearted as those who without to saking (desire) in their heart, falsely take the appearance of those who have forsaken (it)

pope: Outward, they shine as 'kunri' berry's scarlet bright; Inward, like tip of 'kunri' bead, as black as night
drewLazarus: (The world) contains persons whose outside appears (as fair) as the (red) berry of the Abrus, but whose inside is as black as the nose of that berry

pope: Many wash in hollowed waters, living lives of hidden shame; Foul in heart, yet high upraised of men in virtuous fame
drewLazarus: There are many men of masked conduct, who perform their ablutions, and (make a show) of

pope: Cruel is the arrow straight, the crooked lute is sweet, Judge by their deeds the many forms of men you meet
drewLazarus: As, in its use, the arrow is crooked, and the curved lute is straight, so by their deeds, (and not by their appearance) let (the uprightness or crookedness of) men be estimated

pope: What's the worth of shaven head or tresses long, If you shun what all the world condemns as wrong
drewLazarus: There is no need of a shaven crown, nor of tangled hair, if a man abstain from those deeds which the wise have condemned

pope: Who seeks heaven's joys, from impious levity secure, Let him from every fraud preserve his spirit pure
drewLazarus: Let him, who desires not to be despised, keep his mind from (the desire of) defrauding another of the smallest thing

pope: 'Tis sin if in the mind man but thought conceive;'By fraud I will my neighbour of his wealth bereave.'
drewLazarus: Even the thought (of sin) is sin; think not then of crafiily stealing the property of another

pope: The gain that comes by fraud, although it seems to growWith limitless increase, to ruin swift shall go
drewLazarus: The property, which is acquired by fraud, will entirely perish, even while it seems to increase

pope: The lust inveterate of fraudful gain, Yields as its fruit undying pain
drewLazarus: The eager desire of defrauding others will, when it brings forth its fruit, produce undying sorrow

pope: 'Grace' is not in their thoughts, nor know they kind affection's power, Who neighbour's goods desire, and watch for his unguarded hour
drewLazarus: The study of kindness and the exercise of benevolence is not with those who watch for another's forgetfulness, though desire of his property

pope: They cannot walk restrained in wisdom's measured bound, In whom inveterate lust of fraudful gain is found
drewLazarus: They cannot walk steadfastly, according to rule, who eagerly desire to defraud others

pope: Practice of fraud's dark cunning arts they shun, Who long for power by 'measured wisdom' won
drewLazarus: That black-knowledge which is called fraud, is not in those who desire that greatness which is called rectitude

pope: As virtue dwells in heart that 'measured wisdom' gains; Deceit in hearts of fraudful men established reigns
drewLazarus: Deceit dwells in the mind of those who are conversant with fraud, even as virtue in the minds of those who are conversant with rectitude

pope: Who have no lore save that which fraudful arts supply, Acts of unmeasured vice committing straightway die
drewLazarus: Those, who are acquainted with nothing but fraud, will perish in the very commission of transgression

pope: The fraudful forfeit life and being here below; Who fraud eschew the bliss of heavenly beings know
drewLazarus: Even their body will fail the fraudulent; but even the world of the gods will not fail those who are free from fraud

pope: You ask, in lips of men what 'truth' may be;'Tis speech from every taint of evil free
drewLazarus: Truth is the speaking of such words as are free from the least degree of evil (to others)

pope: Falsehood may take the place of truthful word, If blessing, free from fault, it can afford
drewLazarus: Even falsehood has the nature of truth, if it confer a benefit that is free from fault

pope: Speak not a word which false thy own heart knowsSelf-kindled fire within the false one's spirit glows
drewLazarus: Let not a man knowingly tell a lie; for after he has told the lie, his mind will burn him (with the memory of his guilt)

pope: True to his inmost soul who lives,- enshrinedHe lives in souls of all mankind
drewLazarus: He who, in his conduct, preserves a mind free from deceit, will dwell in the minds of all men

pope: Greater is he who speaks the truth with full consenting mindThan men whose lives have penitence and charity combined
drewLazarus: He, who speaks truth with all his heart, is superior to those who make gifts and practise austerities

pope: No praise like that of words from falsehood free; This every virtue yields spontaneously
drewLazarus: There is no praise like the praise of never uttering a falsehood: without causing any suffering, it will lead to every virtue

pope: If all your life be utter truth, the truth alone,'Tis well, though other virtuous acts be left undone
drewLazarus: If a man has the power to abstain from falsehood, it will be well with him, even though he practise no other virtue

pope: Outward purity the water will bestow; Inward purity from truth alone will flow
drewLazarus: Purity of body is produced by water and purity of mind by truthfulness

pope: Every lamp is not a lamp in wise men's sight; That's the lamp with truth's pure radiance bright
drewLazarus: All lamps of nature are not lamps; the lamp of truth is the lamp of the wise

pope: Of all good things we've scanned with studious care, There's nought that can with truthfulness compare
drewLazarus: Amidst all that we have seen (described) as real (excellence), there is nothing so good as truthfulness

pope: Where thou hast power thy angry will to work, thy wrath restrain; Where power is none, what matter if thou check or give it rein
drewLazarus: He restrains his anger who restrains it when it can injure; when it cannot injure, what does it matter whether he restrain it, or not ?

pope: Where power is none to wreak thy wrath, wrath importent is ill; Where thou hast power thy will to work, 'tis greater, evil still
drewLazarus: Anger is bad, even when it cannot injure; when it can injure; there is no greater evil

pope: If any rouse thy wrath, the trespass straight forget; For wrath an endless train of evils will beget
drewLazarus: Forget anger towards every one, as fountains of evil spring from it

pope: Wrath robs the face of smiles, the heart of joy, What other foe to man works such annoy
drewLazarus: What other foe to man works such annoy?

pope: If thou would'st guard thyself, guard against wrath alway;'Gainst wrath who guards not, him his wrath shall slay
drewLazarus: If a man would guard himself, let him guard against anger; if he do not guard it, anger will kill him

pope: Wrath, the fire that slayeth whose draweth near, Will burn the helpful 'raft' of kindred dear
drewLazarus: The fire of anger will burn up even the pleasant raft of friendship

pope: The hand that smites the earth unfailing feels the sting; So perish they who nurse their wrath as noble thing
drewLazarus: Destruction will come upon him who ragards anger as a good thing, as surely as the hand of him who strikes the ground will not fail

pope: Though men should work thee woe, like touch of tongues of fire'Tis well if thou canst save thy soul from burning ire
drewLazarus: Though one commit things against you as painful (to bear) as if a bundle of fire had been thrust upon you, it will be well, to refrain, if possible, from anger

pope: If man his soul preserve from wrathful fires, He gains with that whate'er his soul desires
drewLazarus: If a man never indulges anger in his heart, he will at once obtain whatever he has thought of

pope: Men of surpassing wrath are like the men who've passed away; Who wrath renounce, equals of all-renouncing sages they
drewLazarus: Those, who give way to excessive anger, are no better than dead men; but those, who are freed from it, are equal to those who are freed (from death)

pope: Though ill to neighbour wrought should glorious pride of wealth secure, No ill to do is fixed decree of men in spirit pure
drewLazarus: It is the determination of the spotless not to cause sorrow to others, although they could (by so causing) obtain the wealth which confers greatness

pope: Though malice work its worst, planning no ill return, to endure, And work no ill, is fixed decree of men in spirit pure
drewLazarus: It is the determination of the spotless not to do evil, even in return, to those who have cherished enmity and done them evil

pope: Though unprovoked thy soul malicious foes should sting, Retaliation wrought inevitable woes will bring
drewLazarus: In an ascetic inflict suffering even on those who hate him, when he has not done them any evil, it will afterwards give him irretrievable sorrow

pope: To punish wrong, with kindly benefits the doers ply; Thus shame their souls; but pass the ill unheeded by
drewLazarus: The (proper) punishment to those who have done evil (to you), is to put them to shame by showing them kindness, in return and to forget both the evil and the good done on both sides

pope: From wisdom's vaunted lore what doth the learner gain, If as his own he guard not others' souls from pain
drewLazarus: What benefit has he derived from his knowledge, who does not endeavour to keep off pain from another as much as from himself ?

pope: What his own soul has felt as bitter pain, From making others feel should man abstain
drewLazarus: Let not a man consent to do those things to another which, he knows, will cause sorrow

pope: To work no wilful woe, in any wise, through all the days, To any living soul, is virtue's highest praise
drewLazarus: It is the chief of all virtues not knowingly to do any person evil, even in the lowest degree, and at any time

pope: Whose soul has felt the bitter smart of wrong, how canHe wrongs inflict on ever-living soul of man
drewLazarus: Why does a man inflict upon other creatures those sufferings, which he has found by experience are sufferings to himself ?

pope: If, ere the noontide, you to others evil do, Before the eventide will evil visit you
drewLazarus: If a man inflict sorrow upon others in the morning, it will come upon him unsought in the very evening

pope: O'er every evil-doer evil broodeth still; He evil shuns who freedom seeks from ill
drewLazarus: Sorrow will come upon those who cause pain to others; therfore those, who desire to be free from sorrow, give no pain to others

pope: What is the work of virtue? 'Not to kill'; For 'killing' leads to every work of ill
drewLazarus: Never to destroy life is the sum of all virtuous conduct The destruction of life leads to every evil

pope: Let those that need partake your meal; guard every-thing that lives; This the chief and sum of lore that hoarded wisdom gives
drewLazarus: The chief of all (the virtues) which authors have summed up, is the partaking of food that has been shared with others, and the preservation of the mainfold life of other creatures

pope: Alone, first of goods things, is 'not to slay'; The second is, no untrue word to say
drewLazarus: Not to destroy life is an incomparably (great) good next to it in goodness ranks freedom from falsehood

pope: You ask, What is the good and perfect way?'Tis path of him who studies nought to slay
drewLazarus: Good path is that which considers how it may avoid killing any creature

pope: Of those who 'being' dread, and all renounce, the chief are they, Who dreading crime of slaughter, study nought to slay
drewLazarus: Of all those who, fearing the permanence of earthly births, have abandoned desire, he is the chief who, fearing (the guilt of) murder, considers how he may avoid the destruction of life

pope: Ev'n death that life devours, their happy days shall spare, Who law, 'Thou shall not kill', uphold with reverent care
drewLazarus: Yama, the destroyer of life, will not attack the life of him, who acts under the determination of never destroying life

pope: Though thine own life for that spared life the price must pay, Take not from aught that lives gift of sweet life away
drewLazarus: Let no one do that which would destroy the life of another, although he should by so doing, lose his own life

pope: Though great the gain of good should seem, the wiseWill any gain by staughter won despise
drewLazarus: The advantage which might flow from destroying life in sacrifice, is dishonourable to the wise (who renounced the world), even although it should be said to be productive of great good

pope: Whose trade is 'killing', always vile they show, To minds of them who what is vileness know
drewLazarus: To minds of them who what is vileness know

pope: Who lead a loathed life in bodies sorely pained, Are men, the wise declare, by guilt of slaughter stained
drewLazarus: (The wise) will say that men of diseased bodies, who live in degradation and in poverty, are those who separated the life from the body of animals (in a former birth)

pope: Lowest and meanest lore, that bids men trust secure, In things that pass away, as things that shall endure
drewLazarus: That ignorance which considers those things to be stable which are not so, is dishonourable (to the wise)

pope: As crowds round dancers fill the hall, is wealth's increase; Its loss, as throngs dispersing, when the dances cease
drewLazarus: The acquisition of wealth is like the gathering together of an assembly for a theatre; its expenditure is like the breaking up of that assembly

pope: Unenduring is all wealth; if you wealth enjoy, Enduring works in working wealth straightway employ
