drewLazarus: Wealth is perishable; let those who obtain it immediately practise those (virtues) which are imperishable

pope: As 'day' it vaunts itself; well understood, 'tis knife', That daily cuts away a portion from thy life
drewLazarus: Time, which shows itself (to the ignorant) as if it were something (real) is in the estimation of the wise (only) a saw which cuts down life

pope: Before the tongue lie powerless, 'mid the gasp of gurgling breath, Arouse thyself, and do good deeds beyond the power of death
drewLazarus: Let virtuous deeds be done quickly, before the hiccup comes making the tongue silent

pope: Existing yesterday, today to nothing hurled!-Such greatness owns this transitory world
drewLazarus: This world possesses the greatness that one who yesterday was is not today

pope: Who know not if their happy lives shall last the day, In fancies infinite beguile the hours away
drewLazarus: Innumerable are the thoughts which occupy the mind of (the unwise), who know not that they shall live another moment

pope: Birds fly away, and leave the nest deserted bare; Such is the short-lived friendship soul and body share
drewLazarus: The love of the soul to the body is like (the love of) a bird to its egg which it flies away from and leaves empty

pope: Death is sinking into slumbers deep; Birth again is waking out of sleep
drewLazarus: Death is like sleep; birth is like awaking from it

pope: The soul in fragile shed as lodger courts repose:-Is it because no home's conclusive rest it knows
drewLazarus: It seems as if the soul, which takes a temporary shelter in a body, had not attained a home

pope: From whatever, aye, whatever, man gets free, From what, aye, from that, no more of pain hath he
drewLazarus: Whatever thing, a man has renounced, by that thing; he cannot suffer pain

pope: 'Renunciation' made- ev'n here true pleasures men acquire;'Renounce' while time is yet, if to those pleasures you aspire
drewLazarus: After a man has renounced (all things), there will still be many things in this world (which he may enjoy); if he should desire them, let him, while it is time abandon (the world)

pope: 'Perceptions of the five' must all expire;-Relinquished in its order each desire
drewLazarus: Let the five senses be destroyed; and at the same time, let everything be abandoned that (the ascetic) has (formerly) desired

pope: 'Privation absolute' is penance true;'Possession' brings bewilderment anew
drewLazarus: To be altogether destitute is the proper condition of those who perform austerities; if they possess anything, it will change (their resolution) and bring them back to their confused state

pope: To those who sev'rance seek from being's varied strife, Flesh is burthen sore; what then other bonds of life
drewLazarus: What means the addition of other things those who are attempting to cut off (future) births, when even their body is too much (for them)

pope: Who kills conceit that utters 'I' and 'mine', Shall enter realms above the powers divine
drewLazarus: Shall enter realms above the powers divine

pope: Who cling to things that cling and eager clasp, Griefs cling to them with unrelaxing grasp
drewLazarus: Sorrows will never let go their hold of those who give not up their hold of desire

pope: Who thoroughly 'renounce' on highest height are set; The rest bewildered, lie entangled in the net
drewLazarus: Those who have entirely renounced (all things and all desire) have obtained (absorption into God); all others wander in confusion, entangled in the net of (many) births

pope: When that which clings falls off, severed is being's tie; All else will then be seen as instability
drewLazarus: At the moment in which desire has been abandoned, (other) births will be cut off; when that has not been done, instability will be seen

pope: Cling thou to that which He, to Whom nought clings, hath bid thee cling, Cling to that bond, to get thee free from every clinging thing
drewLazarus: Desire the desire of Him who is without desire; in order to renounce desire, desire that desire

pope: Of things devoid of truth as real things men deem;-Cause of degraded birth the fond delusive dream
drewLazarus: Inglorious births are produced by the confusion (of mind) which considers those things to be real which are not real

pope: Darkness departs, and rapture springs to men who see, The mystic vision pure, from all delusion free
drewLazarus: A clear, undimmed vision of things will deliver its possessors from the darkness of future births, and confer the felicity (of heaven)

pope: When doubts disperse, and mists of error rollAway, nearer is heav'n than earth to sage's soul
drewLazarus: Heaven is nearer than earth to those men of purified minds who are freed from from doubt

pope: Five-fold perception gained, what benefits accrueTo them whose spirits lack perception of the true
drewLazarus: Even those who have all the knowledge which can be attained by the five senses, will derive no benefit from it, if they are without a knowledge of the true nature of things

pope: Whatever thing, of whatsoever kind it be,'Tis wisdom's part in each the very thing to see
drewLazarus: (True) knowledge is the perception concerning every thing of whatever kind, that that thing is the true thing

pope: Who learn, and here the knowledge of the true obtain, Shall find the path that hither cometh not again
drewLazarus: They, who in this birth have learned to know the True Being, enter the road which returns not into this world

pope: The mind that knows with certitude what is, and ponders well, Its thoughts on birth again to other life need not to dwell
drewLazarus: Let it not be thought that there is another birth for him whose mind having thoroughly considered (all it has been taught) has known the True Being

pope: When folly, cause of births, departs; and soul can viewThe truth of things, man's dignity- 'tis wisdom true
drewLazarus: True knowledge consists in the removal of ignorance; which is (the cause of) births, and the perception of the True Being who is (the bestower of) heaven

pope: The true 'support' who knows- rejects 'supports' he sought before-Sorrow that clings all destroys, shall cling to him no more
drewLazarus: He who so lives as to know Him who is the support of all things and abandon all desire, will be freed from the evils which would otherwise cleave to him and destroy (his efforts after absorption)

pope: When lust and wrath and error's triple tyranny is o'er, Their very names for aye extinct, then pain shall be no more
drewLazarus: If the very names of these three things, desire, anger, and confusion of mind, be destroyed, then will also perish evils (which flow from them)

pope: The wise declare, through all the days, to every living thingThat ceaseless round of birth from seed of strong desire doth spring
drewLazarus: (The wise) say that the seed, which produces unceasing births, at all times, to all creatures, is desire

pope: If desire you feel, freedom from changing birth require!'I' will come, if you desire to 'scape, set free from all desire
drewLazarus: If anything be desired, freedom from births should be desired; that (freedom from births) will be attained by desiring to be without desire

pope: No glorious wealth is here like freedom from desire; To bliss like this not even there can soul aspire
drewLazarus: There is in this world no excellence equal to freedom from desire; and even in that world, there is nothing like it

pope: Desire's decease as purity men know; That, too, from yearning search for truth will grow
drewLazarus: Purity (of mind) consists in freedom from desire; and that (freedom from desire) is the fruit of the love of truth

pope: Men freed from bonds of strong desire are free; None other share such perfect liberty
drewLazarus: They are said to be free (from future birth) who are freed from desire; all others (who, whatever else they may be free from, are not freed from desire) are not thus free

pope: Desire each soul beguiles; True virtue dreads its wiles
drewLazarus: It is the chief duty of (an ascetic) to watch against desire with (jealous) fear; for it has power to deceive (and destroy) him

pope: Who thoroughly rids his life of passion-prompted deed, Deeds of unfailing worth shall do, which, as he plans, succeed
drewLazarus: If a man thoroughly cut off all desire, the deeds, which confer immortality, will come to him, in the path in which he seeks them

pope: Affliction is not known where no desires abide; Where these are, endless rises sorrow's tide
drewLazarus: There is no sorrow to those who are without desire; but where that is, (sorrow) will incessantly come, more and more

pope: When dies away desire, that woe of woesEv'n here the soul unceasing rapture knows
drewLazarus: Even while in this body, joy will never depart (from the mind, in which) desire, that sorrow of sorrows, has been destroyed

pope: Drive from thy soul desire insatiate; Straight'way is gained the moveless blissful state
drewLazarus: The removal of desire, whose nature it is never to be satisfied, will immediately confer a nature that can never be changed

pope: Wealth-giving fate power of unflinching effort brings; From fate that takes away idle remissness springs
drewLazarus: Perseverance comes from a prosperous fate, and idleness from an adverse fate

pope: The fate that loss ordains makes wise men's wisdom foolishness; The fate that gain bestows with ampler powers will wisdom bless
drewLazarus: An adverse fate produces folly, and a prosperous fate produces enlarged knowledge

pope: In subtle learning manifold though versed man be,'The wisdom, truly his, will gain supremacy
drewLazarus: Although (a man) may study the most polished treatises, the knowledge which fate has decreed to him will still prevail

pope: Two fold the fashion of the world: some live in fortune's light; While other some have souls in wisdom's radiance bright
drewLazarus: There are (through fate) two different natures in the world, hence the difference (observable in men) in (their acquisition of) wealth, and in their attainment of knowledge

pope: All things that good appear will oft have ill success; All evil things prove good for gain of happiness
drewLazarus: In the acquisition of property, every thing favourable becomes unfavourable, and (on the other hand) everything unfavourable becomes favourable, (through the power of fate)

pope: Things not your own will yield no good, howe'er you guard with pain; Your own, howe'er you scatter them abroad, will yours remain
drewLazarus: Whatever is not conferred by fate cannot be preserved although it be guarded with most painful care; and that, which fate has made his, cannot be lost, although one should even take it and throw it away

pope: Save as the 'sharer' shares to each in due degree, To those who millions store enjoyment scarce can be
drewLazarus: Even those who gather together millions will only enjoy them, as it has been determined by the disposer (of all things)

pope: The destitute with ascetics merit share, If fate to visit with predestined ills would spare
drewLazarus: The destitute will renounce desire (and become ascetics), if (fate) do not make them suffer the hindrances to which they are liable, and they pass away

pope: When good things come, men view them all as gain; When evils come, why then should they complain
drewLazarus: How is it that those, who are pleased with good fortune, trouble themselves when evil comes, (since both are equally the decree of fate) ?

pope: What powers so great as those of Destiny? Man's skillSome other thing contrives; but fate's beforehand still
drewLazarus: What is stronger than fate ? If we think of an expedient (to avert it), it will itself be with us before (the thought)

pope: An army, people, wealth, a minister, friends, fort: six things-Who owns them all, a lion lives amid the kings
drewLazarus: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends and a fortress, is a lion among kings

pope: Courage, a liberal hand, wisdom, and energy: these fourAre qualities a king adorn for evermore
drewLazarus: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character

pope: A sleepless promptitude, knowledge, decision strong:These three for aye to rulers of the land belong
drewLazarus: These three things, viz, vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country

pope: Kingship, in virtue failing not, all vice restrains, In courage failing not, it honour's grace maintains
drewLazarus: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice

pope: A king is he who treasure gains, stores up, defends, And duly for his kingdom's weal expends
drewLazarus: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it

pope: Where king is easy of access, where no harsh word repels, That land's high praises every subject swells
drewLazarus: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language

pope: With pleasant speech, who gives and guards with powerful liberal hand, He sees the world obedient all to his command
drewLazarus: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him

pope: Who guards the realm and justice strict maintains, That king as god o'er subject people reigns
drewLazarus: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).

pope: The king of worth, who can words bitter to his ear endure, Beneath the shadow of his power the world abides secure
drewLazarus: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear

pope: Gifts, grace, right sceptre, care of people's weal; These four a light of dreaded kings reveal
drewLazarus: He is the light of kings who has there four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people

pope: So learn that you may full and faultless learning gain, Then in obedience meet to lessons learnt remain
drewLazarus: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn, and let his conduct be worthy of his learning

pope: The twain that lore of numbers and of letters giveAre eyes, the wise declare, to all on earth that live
drewLazarus: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man

pope: Men who learning gain have eyes, men say; Blockheads' faces pairs of sores display
drewLazarus: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face

pope: You meet with joy, with pleasant thought you part; Such is the learned scholar's wonderous art
drewLazarus: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again.)

pope: With soul submiss they stand, as paupers front a rich man's face; Yet learned men are first; th'unlearned stand in lowest place
drewLazarus: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy

pope: In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow
drewLazarus: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning

pope: The learned make each land their own, in every city find a home; Who, till they die; learn nought, along what weary ways they roam
drewLazarus: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country), and every town his own (town) ?

pope: The man who store of learning gains, In one, through seven worlds, bliss attains
drewLazarus: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births

pope: Their joy is joy of all the world, they see; thus moreThe learners learn to love their cherished lore
drewLazarus: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it

pope: Learning is excellence of wealth that none destroy; To man nought else affords reality of joy
drewLazarus: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches

pope: Like those at draughts would play without the chequered square, Men void of ample lore would counsels of the learned share
drewLazarus: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares

pope: Like those who doat on hoyden's undeveloped charms are they, Of learning void, who eagerly their power of words display
drewLazarus: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of ) woman-hood

pope: The blockheads, too, may men of worth appear, If they can keep from speaking where the learned hear
drewLazarus: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned

pope: From blockheads' lips, when words of wisdom glibly flow, The wise receive them not, though good they seem to show
drewLazarus: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge

pope: As worthless shows the worth of man unlearned, When council meets, by words he speaks discerned
drewLazarus: The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of

pope: 'They are': so much is true of men untaught; But, like a barren field, they yield us nought
drewLazarus: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist

pope: Who lack the power of subtle, large, and penetrating sense, Like puppet, decked with ornaments of clay, their beauty's vain pretence
drewLazarus: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll

pope: To men unlearned, from fortune's favour greater-evil springsThan poverty to men of goodly wisdom brings
drewLazarus: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned

pope: Lower are men unlearned, though noble be their race, Than low-born men adorned with learning's grace
drewLazarus: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned; though they may have been born in a low caste

pope: Learning's irradiating grace who gain, Others excel, as men the bestial train
drewLazarus: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works

pope: Wealth of wealth is wealth acquired be ear attent; Wealth mid all wealth supremely excellent
drewLazarus: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth

pope: When 'tis no longer time the listening ear to feedWith trifling dole of food supply the body's need
drewLazarus: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach

pope: Who feed their ear with learned teachings rare, Are like the happy gods oblations rich who share
drewLazarus: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices

pope: Though learning none hath he, yet let him hear alway:In weakness this shall prove a staff and stay
drewLazarus: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity

pope: Like staff in hand of him in slippery ground who straysAre words from mouth of those who walk in righteous ways
drewLazarus: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place

pope: Let each man good things learn, for e'en as heShall learn, he gains increase of perfect dignity
drewLazarus: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity

pope: Not e'en through inadvertence speak they foolish word, With clear discerning mind who've learning's ample lessons heard
drewLazarus: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied and diligently listened (to instruction)

pope: Where teaching hath not oped the learner's ear, The man may listen, but he scarce can hear
drewLazarus: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf

pope: 'Tis hard for mouth to utter gentle, modest word, When ears discourse of lore refined have never heard
drewLazarus: It is a rare thing to find modesty, a reverend mouth- with those who have not received choice instruction

pope: His mouth can taste, but ear no taste of joy can give!What matter if he die, or prosperous live
drewLazarus: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear ?

pope: True wisdom wards off woes, A circling fortress high; Its inner strength man's eager foes Unshaken will defy
drewLazarus: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy

pope: Wisdom restrains, nor suffers mind to wander where it would; From every evil calls it back, and guides in way of good
drewLazarus: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom

pope: Though things diverse from divers sages' lips we learn,'Tis wisdom's part in each the true thing to discern
drewLazarus: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom

pope: Wisdom hath use of lucid speech, words that acceptance win, And subtle sense of other men's discourse takes in
drewLazarus: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom

pope: Wisdom embraces frank the world, to no caprice exposed; Unlike the lotus flower, now opened wide, now petals strictly closed
drewLazarus: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus flower)

pope: As dwells the world, so with the world to dwellIn harmony- this is to wisely live and well
drewLazarus: To live as the world lives, is wisdom

pope: The wise discern, the foolish fail to see, And minds prepare for things about to be
drewLazarus: The wise are those who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise

pope: Folly meets fearful ills with fearless heart; To fear where cause of fear exists is wisdom's part
drewLazarus: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared

pope: The wise with watchful soul who coming ills foresee; From coming evil's dreaded shock are free
drewLazarus: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils

pope: The wise is rich, with ev'ry blessing blest; The fool is poor, of everything possessed
drewLazarus: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing

pope: Who arrogance, and wrath, and littleness of low desire restrain, To sure increase of lofty dignity attain
drewLazarus: Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust

pope: A niggard hand, o'erweening self-regard, and mirthUnseemly, bring disgrace to men of kingly brith
drewLazarus: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures are faults in a king

pope: Though small as millet-seed the fault men deem; As palm tree vast to those who fear disgrace 'twill seem
drewLazarus: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree

pope: Freedom from faults is wealth; watch heedfully'Gainst these, for fault is fatal enmity
drewLazarus: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy

pope: His joy who guards not 'gainst the coming evil day, Like straw before the fire shall swift consume away
drewLazarus: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like straw before fire

pope: Faultless the king who first his own faults cures, and thenPermits himself to scan faults of other men
drewLazarus: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others

pope: Who leaves undone what should be done, with niggard mind, His wealth shall perish, leaving not a wrack behind
drewLazarus: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it will waste away and not continue

pope: The greed of soul that avarice men call, When faults are summed, is worst of all
drewLazarus: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone - greater than all)

pope: Never indulge in self-complaisant mood, Nor deed desire that yields no gain of good
drewLazarus: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; let him not desire to do useless things

pope: If, to your foes unknown, you cherish what you love, Counsels of men who wish you harm will harmless prove
drewLazarus: If (a king) enjoys, privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless

pope: As friends the men who virtue know, and riper wisdom share, Their worth weighed well, the king should choose with care
drewLazarus: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge

pope: Cherish the all-accomplished men as friends, Whose skill the present ill removes, from coming ill defends
drewLazarus: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen

pope: To cherish men of mighty soul, and make them all their own, Of kingly treasures rare, as rarest gift is known
drewLazarus: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things

pope: To live with men of greatness that their own excels, As cherished friends, is greatest power that with a monarch dwells
drewLazarus: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself is of all powers the highest

pope: The king, since counsellors are monarch's eyes, Should counsellors select with counsel wise
drewLazarus: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them

pope: The king, who knows to live with worthy men allied, Has nought to fear from any foeman's pride
drewLazarus: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men

pope: What power can work his fall, who faithful ministersEmploys, that thunder out reproaches when he errs
drewLazarus: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him ?

pope: The king with none to censure him, bereft of safeguards all, Though none his ruin work, shall surely ruined fall
drewLazarus: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him

pope: Who owns no principal, can have no gain of usury; Who lacks support of friends, knows no stability
drewLazarus: There can be no gain to those who have no capital; and in like manner there can be no permanence to

pope: Than hate of many foes incurred, works greater woeTen-fold, of worthy men the friendship to forego
drewLazarus: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many

pope: The great of soul will mean association fear; The mean of soul regard mean men as kinsmen dear
drewLazarus: (True) greatness fears the society of the base; it is only the low - minded who will regard them as friends

pope: The waters' virtues change with soil through which they flow; As man's companionship so will his wisdom show
drewLazarus: As water changes (its nature), from the nature of the soil (in which it flows), so will the character of men resemble that of their associates

pope: Perceptions manifold in men are of the mind alone; The value of the man by his companionship is known
drewLazarus: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates

pope: Man's wisdom seems the offspring of his mind;'Tis outcome of companionship we find
drewLazarus: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions

pope: Both purity of mind, and purity of action clear, Leaning no staff of pure companionship, to man draw near
drewLazarus: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz, purity of mind and purity of conduct

pope: From true pure-minded men a virtuous race proceeds; To men of pure companionship belong no evil deeds
drewLazarus: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good

pope: Goodness of mind to lives of men increaseth gain; And good companionship doth all of praise obtain
drewLazarus: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men

pope: To perfect men, though minds right good belong, Yet good companionship is confirmation strong
drewLazarus: Yet good companionship is confirmation strong

pope: Although to mental goodness joys of other life belong, Yet good companionship is confirmation strong
drewLazarus: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good

pope: Than good companionship no surer help we know; Than bad companionship nought causes direr woe
drewLazarus: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked

pope: Expenditure, return, and profit of the deedIn time to come; weigh these- than to the act proceed
drewLazarus: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act

pope: With chosen friends deliberate; next use the private thought; Then act By those who thus proceed all works with ease are wrought
drewLazarus: There is nothing too difficult to (be attained by) those who, before they act, reflect well themselves, and thoroughly consider (the matter) with chosen friends

pope: To risk one's all and lose, aiming at added gain, Is rash affair, from which the wise abstain
drewLazarus: Wise men will not, in the hopes of profit, undertake works that will consume their principal

pope: A work of which the issue is not clear, Begin not they reproachful scorn who fear
drewLazarus: Those who fear reproach will not commence anything which has not been (thoroughly considered) and made clear to them

pope: With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow
drewLazarus: One way to promote the prosperity of an enemy, is (for a king) to set out (to war) without having thoroughly weighed his ability (to cope with its chances)

pope: 'Tis ruin if man do an unbefitting thing; Fit things to leave undone will equal ruin bring
drewLazarus: He will perish who does not what is not fit to do; and he also will perish who does not do what it is fit to

pope: Think, and then dare the deed! Who cry,'Deed dared, we'll think,' disgraced shall be
drewLazarus: Consider, and then undertake a matter; after having undertaken it, to say "We will consider," is folly

pope: On no right system if man toil and strive, Though many men assist, no work can thrive
drewLazarus: The work, which is not done by suitable methods, will fail though many stand to uphold it

pope: Though well the work be done, yet one mistake is made, To habitudes of various men when no regard is paid
drewLazarus: There are failures even in acting well, when it is done without knowing the various dispositions of men

pope: Plan and perform no work that others may despise; What misbeseems a king the world will not approve as wise
drewLazarus: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things which do not become of his position to adopt

pope: The force the strife demands, the force he owns, the force of foes, The force of friends; these should he weigh ere to the war he goes
drewLazarus: Let (one) weigh well the strength of the deed (he purposes to do), his own strength, the strength of his enemy, and the strength of the allies (of both), and then let him act

pope: Who know what can be wrought, with knowledge of the means, on this, Their mind firm set, go forth, nought goes with them amiss
drewLazarus: There is nothing which may not be accomplished by those who, before they attack (an enemy), make themselves acquainted with their own ability, and with whatever else is (needful) to be known, and

pope: Ill-deeming of their proper powers, have many monarchs striven, And midmost of unequal conflict fallen asunder riven
drewLazarus: There are many who, ignorant of their (want of) power (to meet it), have haughtily set out to war, and broken down in the midst of it

pope: Who not agrees with those around, no moderation knows, In self-applause indulging, swift to ruin goes
drewLazarus: He will quickly perish who, ignorant of his own resources flatters himself of his greatness, and does

pope: With peacock feathers light, you load the wain; Yet, heaped too high, the axle snaps in twain
drewLazarus: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks' feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded

pope: Who daring climbs, and would himself upraiseBeyond the branch's tip, with life the forfeit pays
drewLazarus: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further

pope: With knowledge of the measure due, as virtue bids you give!That is the way to guard your wealth, and seemly live
drewLazarus: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give), and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property

pope: Incomings may be scant; but yet, no failure there, If in expenditure you rightly learn to spare
drewLazarus: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income

pope: Who prosperous lives and of enjoyment knows no bound, His seeming wealth, departing, nowhere shall be found
drewLazarus: The prosperity of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue

pope: Beneficence that measures not its bound of means, Will swiftly bring to nought the wealth on which it leans
drewLazarus: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property

pope: A crow will conquer owl in broad daylight; The king that foes would crush, needs fitting time to fight
drewLazarus: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time

pope: The bond binds fortune fast is ordered effort made, Strictly observant still of favouring season's aid
drewLazarus: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king)

pope: Can any work be hard in very fact, If men use fitting means in timely act
drewLazarus: Is there anything difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments at the right time ?

pope: The pendant world's dominion may be won, In fitting time and place by action done
drewLazarus: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it if he acts in the right time, and at the right place

pope: Who think the pendant world itself to subjugate, With mind unruffled for the fitting time must wait
drewLazarus: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action), may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world

pope: The men of mighty power their hidden energies repress, As fighting ram recoils to rush on foe with heavier stress
drewLazarus: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable opportunity), is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt

pope: The glorious once of wrath enkindled make no outward show, At once; they bide their time, while hidden fires within them glow
drewLazarus: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within

pope: If foes' detested form they see, with patience let them bear; When fateful hour at last they spy,- the head lies there
drewLazarus: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily brought low

pope: When hardest gain of opportunity at last is won, With promptitude let hardest deed be done
drewLazarus: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity)

pope: As heron stands with folded wing, so wait in waiting hour; As heron snaps its prey, when fortune smiles, put forth your power
drewLazarus: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity

pope: Begin no work of war, depise no foe, Till place where you can wholly circumvent you know
drewLazarus: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy), nor undertake any thing (against him), until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him

pope: Though skill in war combine with courage tried on battle-field, The added gain of fort doth great advantage yield
drewLazarus: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages

pope: E'en weak ones mightily prevail, if place of strong defence, They find, protect themselves, and work their foes offence
drewLazarus: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies

pope: The foes who thought to triumph, find their thoughts were vain, If hosts advance, seize vantage ground, and thence the fight maintain
drewLazarus: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them

pope: The crocodile prevails in its own flow of water wide, If this it leaves, 'tis slain by anything beside
drewLazarus: In deep water, a crocodile will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it

pope: The lofty car, with mighty wheel, sails not o'er watery main, The boat that skims the sea, runs not on earth's hard plain
drewLazarus: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that the traverse ocean, move on the earth

pope: Save their own fearless might they need no other aid, If in right place they fight, all due provision made
drewLazarus: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations

pope: If lord of army vast the safe retreat assailOf him whose host is small, his mightiest efforts fail
drewLazarus: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act

pope: Though fort be none, and store of wealth they lack,'Tis hard a people's homesteads to attack
drewLazarus: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress

pope: The jackal slays, in miry paths of foot-betraying fen, The elephant of fearless eye and tusks transfixing armed men
drewLazarus: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down

pope: How treats he virtue, wealth and pleasure? How, when life's at stake, Comports himself? This four-fold test of man will full assurance make
drewLazarus: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,-his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and tear of (losing) life

pope: Of noble race, of faultless worth, of generous prideThat shrinks from shame or stain; in him may king confide
drewLazarus: (The king's) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin)

pope: Though deeply learned, unflecked by fault, 'tis rare to see, When closely scanned, a man from all unwisdom free
drewLazarus: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance

pope: Weigh well the good of each, his failings closely scan, As these or those prevail, so estimate the man
drewLazarus: Let (a king) consider (a man's) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails

pope: Of greatness and of meanness too, The deeds of each are touchstone true
drewLazarus: A man's deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness

pope: Beware of trusting men who have no kith of kin; No bonds restrain such men, no shame deters from sin
drewLazarus: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachment, and thereforehave no fear of crime

pope: By fond affection led who trusts in men of unwise soul, Yields all his being up to folly's blind control
drewLazarus: Yields all his being up to folly's blind control

pope: Who trusts an untried stranger, brings disgrace, Remediless, on all his race
drewLazarus: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him chooses a stranger whose character he has not known

pope: Trust no man whom you have not fully tried, When tested, in his prudence proved confide
drewLazarus: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate

pope: Trust where you have not tried, doubt of a friend to feel, Once trusted, wounds inflict that nought can heal
drewLazarus: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce irremediable sorrow

pope: Who good and evil scanning, ever makes the good his joy; Such man of virtuous mood should king employ
drewLazarus: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking

pope: Who swells the revenues, spreads plenty o'er the land, Seeks out what hinders progress, his the workman's hand
drewLazarus: Let him do (the king's) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue), increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it)

pope: A loyal love with wisdom, clearness, mind from avarice free; Who hath these four good gifts should ever trusted be
drewLazarus: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind and freedom from covetousness

pope: Even when tests of every kind are multiplied, Full many a man proves otherwise, by action tried
drewLazarus: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed)

pope: No specious fav'rite should the king's commission bear, But he that knows, and work performs with patient care
drewLazarus: (A king's) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment

pope: Let king first ask, 'Who shall the deed perform?' and 'What the deed?'Of hour befitting both assured, let every work proceed
drewLazarus: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it

pope: 'This man, this work shall thus work out,' let thoughtful king command; Then leave the matter wholly in his servant's hand
drewLazarus: After having considered, "this man can accomplish this, by these means", let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty

pope: As each man's special aptitude is known, Bid each man make that special work his own
drewLazarus: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work

pope: Fortune deserts the king who ill can bear, Informal friendly ways of men his tolls who share
drewLazarus: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties

pope: Let king search out his servants' deeds each day; When these do right, the world goes rightly on its way
drewLazarus: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly

pope: When wealth is fled, old kindness still to show, Is kindly grace that only kinsmen know
drewLazarus: Even when (a man's) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness)

pope: The gift of kin's unfailing love bestowsMuch gain of good, like flower that fadeless blows
drewLazarus: If (a man's) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of everincreasing wealth

pope: His joy of life who mingles not with kinsmen gathered round, Is lake where streams pour in, with no encircling bound
drewLazarus: The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a

pope: The profit gained by wealth's increase, Is living compassed round by relatives in peace
drewLazarus: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth

pope: Who knows the use of pleasant words, and liberal gifts can give, Connections, heaps of them, surrounding him shall live
drewLazarus: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability

pope: Than one who gifts bestows and wrath restrains, Through the wide world none larger following gains
drewLazarus: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gift, and does not give way to anger

pope: The crows conceal not, call their friends to come, then eat; Increase of good such worthy ones shall meet
drewLazarus: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives)

pope: Where king regards not all alike, but each in his degree,'Neath such discerning rule many dwell happily
drewLazarus: Many relatives will live near a king, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit

pope: Who once were his, and then forsook him, as beforeWill come around, when cause of disagreement is no more
drewLazarus: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him

pope: Who causeless went away, then to return, for any cause, ask leave; The king should sift their motives well, consider, and receive
drewLazarus: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again

pope: 'Tis greater ill, it rapture of o'erweening gladness to the soulBring self-forgetfulness than if transcendent wrath control
drewLazarus: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy

pope: Perpetual, poverty is death to wisdom of the wise; When man forgets himself his glory dies
drewLazarus: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge

pope: 'To self-oblivious men no praise'; this ruleDecisive wisdom sums of every school
drewLazarus: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world

pope: 'To cowards is no fort's defence'; e'en soThe self-oblivious men no blessing know
drewLazarus: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications ha may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess)

pope: To him who nought foresees, recks not of anything, The after woe shall sure repentance bring
drewLazarus: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault

pope: Towards all unswerving, ever watchfulness of soul retain, Where this is found there is no greater gain
drewLazarus: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times; and towards all persons

pope: Though things are arduous deemed, there's nought may not be won, When work with mind's unslumbering energy and thought is done
drewLazarus: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour

pope: Let things that merit praise thy watchful soul employ; Who these despise attain through sevenfold births no joy
drewLazarus: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births

pope: Think on the men whom scornful mind hath brought to nought, When exultation overwhelms thy wildered thought
drewLazarus: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy

pope: 'Tis easy what thou hast in mind to gain, If what thou hast in mind thy mind retain
drewLazarus: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it

pope: Search out, to no one favour show; with heart that justice lovesConsult, then act; this is the rule that right approves
drewLazarus: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favour (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on,

pope: All earth looks up to heav'n whence raindrops fall; All subjects look to king that ruleth all
drewLazarus: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive

pope: Learning and virtue of the sages spring, From all-controlling sceptre of the king
drewLazarus: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described

pope: Whose heart embraces subjects all, lord over mighty landWho rules, the world his feet embracing stands
drewLazarus: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love

pope: Where king, who righteous laws regards, the sceptre wields, There fall the showers, there rich abundance crowns the fields
drewLazarus: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice

pope: Not lance gives kings the victory, But sceptre swayed with equity
drewLazarus: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king's sceptre, if it do no injustice

pope: The king all the whole realm of earth protects; And justice guards the king who right respects
drewLazarus: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king

pope: Hard of access, nought searching out, with partial handThe king who rules, shall sink and perish from the land
drewLazarus: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace

pope: Abroad to guard, at home to punish, bringsNo just reproach; 'tis work assigned to kings
drewLazarus: In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself; to punish crime

pope: By punishment of death the cruel to restrain, Is as when farmer frees from weeds the tender grain
drewLazarus: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn

pope: Than one who plies the murderer's trade, more cruel is the kingWho all injustice works, his subjects harassing
drewLazarus: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer

pope: As 'Give' the robber cries with lance uplift, So kings with sceptred hand implore a gift
drewLazarus: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says "give up your wealth"

pope: Who makes no daily search for wrongs, nor justly rules, that kingDoth day by day his realm to ruin bring
drewLazarus: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin

pope: Whose rod from right deflects, who counsel doth refuse, At once his wealth and people utterly shall lose
drewLazarus: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects

pope: His people's tears of sorrow past endurance, are not theySharp instruments to wear the monarch's wealth away
drewLazarus: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth ?

pope: To rulers' rule stability is sceptre right; When this is not, quenched is the rulers' light
drewLazarus: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance

pope: As lack of rain to thirsty lands beneath, Is lack of grace in kings to all that breathe
drewLazarus: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness

pope: To poverty it adds a sharper sting, To live beneath the sway of unjust king
drewLazarus: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice

pope: Where king from right deflecting, makes unrighteous gain, The seasons change, the clouds pour down no rain
drewLazarus: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers

pope: Where guardian guardeth not, udder of kine grows dry, And Brahmans' sacred lore will all forgotten lie
drewLazarus: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six duties viz, the Brahmins will forget the vedas

pope: Who punishes, investigation made in due degree, So as to stay advance of crime, a king is he
drewLazarus: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed

pope: For length of days with still increasing joys on Heav'n who call, Should raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall
drewLazarus: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquires with strictness, and then punish with mildness

pope: Where subjects dread of cruel wrongs endure, Ruin to unjust king is swift and sure
drewLazarus: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin

pope: 'Ah! cruel is our king', where subjects sadly say, His age shall dwindle, swift his joy of life decay
drewLazarus: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish; his life becoming shortened

pope: Whom subjects scarce may see, of harsh forbidding countenance; His ample wealth shall waste, blasted by demon's glance
drewLazarus: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil

pope: The tyrant, harsh in speach and hard of eye, His ample joy, swift fading, soon shall die
drewLazarus: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him

pope: Harsh words and punishments severe beyond the right, Are file that wears away the monarch's conquering might
drewLazarus: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king's power for destroying (his enemies)

pope: Who leaves the work to those around, and thinks of it no more; If he in wrathful mood reprove, his prosperous days are o'er
drewLazarus: The prosperity of that king will waste away, who without reflecting (on his affairs himself), commits them to his ministers, and (when a failure occurs) gives way to anger, and rages against them

pope: Who builds no fort whence he may foe defy, In time of war shall fear and swiftly die
drewLazarus: The king who has not provided himself with a place of defence, will in times of war be seized with fear and quickly perish

pope: Tyrants with fools their counsels share:Earth can no heavier burthen bear
drewLazarus: The earth bears up no greater burden than ignorant men whom a cruel sceptre attaches to itself (as the ministers of its evil deeds)

pope: Since true benignity, that grace exceeding great, residesIn kingly souls, world in happy state abides
drewLazarus: The world exists through that greatest ornament (of princes), a gracious demeanour

pope: The world goes on its wonted way, since grace benign is there; All other men are burthen for the earth to bear
drewLazarus: The prosperity of the world springs from the kindliness, the existence of those who have no (kindliness) is a burden to the earth

pope: Where not accordant with the song, what use of sounding chordsWhat gain of eye that no benignant light affords
drewLazarus: Of what avail is a song if it be inconsistent with harmony ? what is the use of eyes which possess no kindliness

pope: The seeming eye of face gives no expressive light, When not with duly meted kindness bright
drewLazarus: Beyond appearing to be in the face, what good do they do, those eyes in which is no well-regulated kindness ?

pope: Benignity is eyes' adorning grace; Without it eyes are wounds disfiguring face
drewLazarus: Kind looks are the ornaments of the eyes; without these they will be considered (by the wise) to be merely two sores

pope: Whose eyes 'neath brow infixed diffuse no rayOf grace; like tree in earth infixed are they
drewLazarus: They resemble the trees of the earth, who although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others)

pope: Eyeless are they whose eyes with no benignant lustre shine; Who've eyes can never lack the light of grace benign
drewLazarus: Men without kind looks are men without eyes; those who (really) have eyes are also not devoid of kind looks

pope: Who can benignant smile, yet leave no work undone; By them as very own may all the earth be won
drewLazarus: The world is theirs (kings) who are able to show kindness, without injury to their affairs, (administration of justice)

pope: To smile on those that vex, with kindly face, Enduring long, is most excelling grace
drewLazarus: Patiently to bear with, and show kindness to those who grieve us, is the most excellent of all dispositions

pope: They drink with smiling grace, though poison interfused they see, Who seek the praise of all-esteemed courtesy
drewLazarus: Those who desire (to cultivate that degree of) urbanity which all shall love, even after swallowing the poison served to them by their friends, will be friendly with them

pope: These two: the code renowned and spies, In these let king confide as eyes
drewLazarus: Let a king consider as his eyes these two things, a spy and a book (of laws) universally esteemed

pope: Each day, of every subject every deed,'Tis duty of the king to learn with speed
drewLazarus: 'Tis duty of the king to learn with speed

pope: By spies who spies, not weighing things they bring, Nothing can victory give to that unwary king
drewLazarus: There is no way for a king to obtain conquests, who knows not the advantage of discoveries made by a spy

pope: His officers, his friends, his enemies, All these who watch are trusty spies
drewLazarus: He is a spy who watches all men, to wit, those who are in the king's employment, his relatives, and his enemies

pope: Of unsuspected mien and all-unfearing eyes, Who let no secret out, are trusty spies
drewLazarus: A spy is one who is able to assume an appearance which may create no suspicion (in the minds of others), who fears no man's face, and who never reveals (his purpose)

pope: As monk or devotee, through every hindrance making way, A spy, whate'er men do, must watchful mind display
drewLazarus: He is a spy who, assuming the appearance of an ascetic, goes into (whatever place he wishes), examines into (all, that is needful), and never discovers himself, whatever may be done to him

pope: A spy must search each hidden matter out, And full report must render, free from doubt
drewLazarus: A spy is one who is able to discover what is hidden and who retains no doubt concerning what he has known

pope: Spying by spies, the things they tellTo test by other spies is well
drewLazarus: Let not a king receive the information which a spy has discovered and made known to him, until he has examined it by another spy

pope: One spy must not another see: contrive it so; And things by three confirmed as truth you know
drewLazarus: Let a king employ spies so that one may have no knowledge of the other; and when the information of three agrees together, let him receive it

pope: Reward not trusty spy in others' sight, Or all the mystery will come to light
drewLazarus: Let not a king publicly confer on a spy any marks of his favour; if he does, he will divulge his own secret

pope: 'Tis energy gives men o'er that they own a true control; They nothing own who own not energy of soul
drewLazarus: Energy makes out the man of property; as for those who are destitute of it, do they (really) possess what they possess ?

pope: The wealth of mind man owns a real worth imparts, Material wealth man owns endures not, utterly departs
drewLazarus: The possession of (energy of) mind is true property; the possession of wealth passes away and abides not

pope: 'Lost is our wealth,' they utter not this cry distressed, The men of firm concentred energy of soul possessed
drewLazarus: They who are possessed of enduring energy will not trouble themselves, saying, "we have lost our property."

pope: The man of energy of soul inflexible, Good fortune seeks him out and comes a friend to dwell
drewLazarus: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy

pope: With rising flood the rising lotus flower its stem unwinds; The dignity of men is measured by their minds
drewLazarus: The stalks of water-flowers are proportionate to the depth of water; so is men's greatness proportionate to their minds

pope: Whate'er you ponder, let your aim be loftly still, Fate cannot hinder always, thwart you as it will
drewLazarus: In all that a king thinks of, let him think of his greatness; and if it should be thrust from him (by fate), it will have the nature of not being thrust from him

pope: The men of lofty mind quail not in ruin's fateful hour, The elephant retains his dignity mind arrows' deadly shower
drewLazarus: The strong minded will not faint, even when all is lost; the elephant stands firm, even when wounded by a shower of arrows

pope: The soulless man can never gainTh' ennobling sense of power with men
drewLazarus: Those who have no (greatness of) mind, will not acquire the joy of saying in the world, "we have excercised liaberality"

pope: Huge bulk of elephant with pointed tusk all armed, When tiger threatens shrinks away alarmed
drewLazarus: Although the elephant has a large body, and a sharp tusk, yet it fears the attack of the tiger

pope: Firmness of soul in man is real excellance; Others are trees, their human form a mere pretence
drewLazarus: Energy is mental wealth; those men who are destitute of it are only trees in the form of men

pope: Of household dignity the lustre beaming bright, Flickers and dies when sluggish foulness dims its light
drewLazarus: By the darkness, of idleness, the indestructible lamp of family (rank) will be extinguished

pope: Let indolence, the death of effort, die, If you'd uphold your household's dignity
drewLazarus: Let those, who desire that their family may be illustrious, put away all idleness from their conduct

pope: Who fosters indolence within his breast, the silly elf!The house from which he springs shall perish ere himself
drewLazarus: The (lustre of the) family of the ignorant man, who acts under the influence of destructive laziness will perish, even before he is dead

pope: His family decays, and faults unheeded thrive, Who, sunk in sloth, for noble objects doth not strive
drewLazarus: Family (greatness) will be destroyed, and faults will increase, in those men who give way to laziness, and put forth no dignified exertions

pope: Delay, oblivion, sloth, and sleep: these fourAre pleasure-boat to bear the doomed to ruin's shore
drewLazarus: Procrastination, forgetfulness, idleness, and sleep, these four things, form the vessel which is desired by those destined to destruction

pope: Though lords of earth unearned possessions gain, The slothful ones no yield of good obtain
drewLazarus: It is a rare thing for the idle, even when possessed of the riches of kings who ruled over the whole earth, to derive any great benefit from it

pope: Who hug their sloth, nor noble works attempt, Shall bear reproofs and words of just contempt
drewLazarus: Those who through idleness, and do not engage themselves in dignified exertion, will subject

pope: If sloth a dwelling find mid noble family, Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be
drewLazarus: If idleness take up its abode in a king of high birth, it will make him a slave of his enemies

pope: Who changes slothful habits savesHimself from all that household rule depraves
drewLazarus: When a man puts away idleness, the reproach which has come upon himself and his family will disappear

pope: The king whose life from sluggishness is rid, Shall rule o'er all by foot of mighty god bestrid
drewLazarus: The king who never gives way to idleness will obtain entire possession of (the whole earth) passed over by him who measured (the worlds) with His foot

pope: Say not, 'Tis hard', in weak, desponding hour, For strenuous effort gives prevailing power
drewLazarus: Yield not to the feebleness which says, "this is too difficult to be done"; labour will give the greatness (of mind) which is necessary (to do it)

pope: In action be thou, 'ware of act's defeat; The world leaves those who work leave incomplete
drewLazarus: Take care not to give up exertion in the midst of a work; the world will abandon those who abandon their unfinished work

pope: In strenuous effort doth resideThe power of helping others: noble pride
drewLazarus: The lustre of munificence will dwell only with the dignity of laboriousness or efforts

pope: Beneficent intent in men by whom no strenuous work is wrought, Like battle-axe in sexless being's hand availeth nought
drewLazarus: The liberality of him, who does not labour, will fail, like the manliness of a hermaphrodite, who has a sword in its hand

pope: Whose heart delighteth not in pleasure, but in action finds delight, He wipes away his kinsmen's grief and stands the pillar of their might
drewLazarus: He who desires not pleasure, but desires labour, will be a pillar to sustain his relations, wiping away their sorrows

pope: Effort brings fortune's sure increase, Its absence brings to nothingness
drewLazarus: Labour will produce wealth; idleness will bring poverty

pope: In sluggishness is seen misfortune's lurid form, the wise declare; Where man unslothful toils, she of the lotus flower is there
drewLazarus: They say that the black Mudevi (the goddess of adversity) dwells with laziness, and the Latchmi (the goddess of prosperity) dwells with the labour of the industrious

pope: 'Tis no reproach unpropitious fate should ban; But not to do man's work is foul disgrace to man
drewLazarus: Adverse fate is no disgrace to any one; to be without exertion and without knowing what should be known, is disgrace

pope: Though fate-divine should make your labour vain; Effort its labour's sure reward will gain
drewLazarus: Although it be said that, through fate, it cannot be attained, yet labour, with bodily exertion, will yield its reward

pope: Who strive with undismayed, unfaltering mind, At length shall leave opposing fate behind
drewLazarus: They who labour on, without fear and without fainting will see even fate (put) behind their back

pope: Smile, with patient, hopeful heart, in troublous hour; Meet and so vanquish grief; nothing hath equal power
drewLazarus: If troubles come, laugh; there is nothing like that, to press upon and drive away sorrow

pope: Though sorrow, like a flood, comes rolling on, When wise men's mind regards it,- it is gone
drewLazarus: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the (courageous) thought which the minds of the wise will entertain, even in sorrow

pope: Who griefs confront with meek, ungrieving heart, From them griefs, put to grief, depart
drewLazarus: They give sorrow to sorrow, who in sorrow do not suffer sorrow

pope: Like bullock struggle on through each obstructed way; From such an one will troubles, troubled, roll away
drewLazarus: Troubles will vanish (i.e., will be troubled) before the man who (struggles against difficulties) as a

pope: When griefs press on, but fail to crush the patient heart, Then griefs defeated, put to grief, depart
drewLazarus: The troubles of that man will be troubled (and disappear) who, however thickly they may come upon him, does not abandon (his purpose)

pope: Who boasted not of wealth, nor gave it all their heart, Will not bemoan the loss, when prosperous days depart
drewLazarus: Will those men ever cry out in sorrow, "we are destitute" who, (in their prosperity), give not way to (undue desire) to keep their wealth

pope: 'Man's frame is sorrow's target', the noble mind reflects, Nor meets with troubled mind the sorrows it expects
drewLazarus: The great will not regard trouble as trouble, knowing that the body is the butt of trouble

pope: He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows; Such man will walk unharmed by touch of human woes
drewLazarus: That man never experiences sorrow, who does not seek for pleasure, and who considers distress to be natural (to man)

pope: Mid joys he yields not heart to joys' controlMid sorrows, sorrow cannot touch his soul
drewLazarus: He does not suffer sorrow, in sorrow who does not look for pleasure in pleasure

pope: Who pain as pleasure takes, he shall acquireThe bliss to which his foes in vain aspire
drewLazarus: The elevation, which even his enemies will esteem, will be gained by him, who regards pain as pleasure

pope: A minister is he who grasps, with wisdom large, Means, time, work's mode, and functions rare he must discharge
drewLazarus: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the difficult undertaking (itself)

pope: A minister must greatness own of guardian power, determined mind, Learn'd wisdom, manly effort with the former five combined
drewLazarus: The minister is one who in addition to the aforesaid five things excels in the possession of firmness,

pope: A minister is he whose power can foes divide, Attach more firmly friends, of severed ones can heal the breaches wide
drewLazarus: The minister is one who can effect discord (among foes), maintain the good-will of his friends and restore to friendship those who have seceded (from him)

pope: A minister has power to see the methods help afford, To ponder long, then utter calm conclusive word
drewLazarus: The minister is one who is able to comprehend (the whole nature of an undertaking), execute it in the best manner possible, and offer assuring advice (in time of necessity)

pope: The man who virtue knows, has use of wise and pleasant wordsWith plans for every season apt, in counsel aid affords
drewLazarus: He is the best helper (of the king) who understanding the duties, of the latter, is by his special learning, able to tender the fullest advice, and at all times conversant with the best method (of

pope: When native subtilty combines with sound scholastic lore,'Tis subtilty surpassing all, which nothing stands before
drewLazarus: What (contrivances) are there so acute as to resist those who possess natural acuteness in addition to learning ?

pope: Though knowing all that books can teach, 'tis truest tactTo follow common sense of men in act
drewLazarus: Though you are acquainted with the (theoretical) methods (of performing an act), understand the ways of the world and act accordingly

pope: 'Tis duty of the man in place aloud to sayThe very truth, though unwise king may cast his words away
drewLazarus: Although the king be utterly ignorant, it is the duty of the minister to give (him) sound advice

pope: A minister who by king's side plots evil thingsWorse woes than countless foemen brings
drewLazarus: Far better are seventy crores of enemies (for a king) than a minister at his side who intends (his) ruin

pope: For gain of end desired just counsel nought availsTo minister, when tact in execution fails
drewLazarus: Those ministers who are destitute of (executive) ability will fail to carry out their projects, although they may have contrived aright

pope: A tongue that rightly speaks the right is greatest gain, It stands alone midst goodly things that men obtain
drewLazarus: The possession of that goodness which is called the goodness of speech is (even to others) better than any other goodness

pope: Since gain and loss in life on speech depend, From careless slip in speech thyself defend
drewLazarus: Since (both) wealth and evil result from (their) speech, ministers should most carefully guard themselves against faultiness therein

pope: 'Tis speech that spell-bound holds the listening ear, While those who have not heard desire to hear
drewLazarus: The (minister's) speech is that which seeks (to express) elements as bind his friends (to himself) and is so delivered as to make even his enemies desire (his friendship)

pope: Speak words adapted well to various hearers' state; No higher virtue lives, no gain more surely great
drewLazarus: Understand the qualities (of your hearers) and (then) make your speech; for superior to it, there is neither virtue nor wealth

pope: Speak out your speech, when once 'tis past disputeThat none can utter speech that shall your speech refute
drewLazarus: Deliver your speech, after assuring yourself that no counter speech can defeat your own

pope: Charming each hearer's ear, of others' words to seize the sense, Is method wise of men of spotless excellence
drewLazarus: It is the opinion of those who are free from defects in diplomacy that the minister should speak so as to make his hearers desire (to hear more) and grasp the meaning of what he hears himself

pope: Mighty in word, of unforgetful mind, of fearless speech,'Tis hard for hostile power such man to overreach
drewLazarus: It is impossible for any one to conquer him by intrique who possesses power of speech, and is neither faulty nor timid

pope: Swiftly the listening world will gather round, When men of mighty speech the weighty theme propound
drewLazarus: If there be those who can speak on various subjects in their proper order and in a pleasing manner, the world would readily accept them

pope: Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain, Their tongues will itch with thousand words man's ears to pain
drewLazarus: They will desire to utter many words, who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones

pope: Like scentless flower in blooming garland boundAre men who can't their lore acquired to other's ears expound
drewLazarus: Those who are unable to set forth their acquirements (before others) are like flowers blossoming in a cluster and yet without fragrance

pope: The good external help confers is worldly gain; By action good men every needed gift obtain
drewLazarus: The efficacy of support will yield (only) wealth; (but) the efficacy of action will yield all that is desired

pope: From action evermore thyself restrainOf glory and of good that yields no gain
drewLazarus: Ministers should at all times avoid acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit (for the future)

pope: Who tell themselves that nobler things shall yet be wonAll deeds that dim the light of glory must they shun
drewLazarus: Those who say, "we will become (better)" should avoid the performance of acts that would destroy (their fame)

pope: Though troubles press, no shameful deed they do, Whose eyes the ever-during vision view
drewLazarus: Those who have infallible judgement though threatened with peril will not do acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)

pope: Do nought that soul repenting must deplore, If thou hast sinned, 'tis well if thou dost sin no more
drewLazarus: Let a minister never do acts of which he would have to grieve saying, "what is this I have done"; (but) should he do (them), it were good that he grieved not

pope: Though her that bore thee hung'ring thou behold, no deedDo thou, that men of perfect soul have crime decreed
drewLazarus: Though a minister may see his mother starve; let him do not act which the wise would (treat with contempt)

pope: Than store of wealth guilt-laden souls obtain, The sorest poverty of perfect soul is richer gain
drewLazarus: Far more excellent is the extreme poverty of the wise than wealth obtained by heaping up of sinful

pope: To those who hate reproof and do forbidden thingWhat prospers now, in after days shall anguish bring
drewLazarus: The actions of those, who have not desisted from doing deeds forbidden (by the great), will, even if they succeed, cause them sorrow

pope: What's gained through tears with tears shall go; From loss good deeds entail harvests of blessings grow
drewLazarus: All that has been obtained with tears (to the victim) will depart with tears (to himself); but what has been by fair means; though with loss at first, will afterwards yield fruit

pope: In pot of clay unburnt he water pours and would retain, Who seeks by wrong the realm in wealth and safety to maintain
drewLazarus: (For a minister) to protect (his king) with wealth obtained by foul means is like preserving a vessel of wet clay by filling it with water

pope: What men call 'power in action' know for 'power of mind'Externe to man all other aids you find
drewLazarus: Firmness in action is (simply) one's firmness of mind; all other (abilities) are not of this nature

pope: 'Each hindrance shun', 'unyielding onward press, If obstacle be there,'These two define your way, so those that search out truth declare
drewLazarus: Not to perform a ruinous act, and not to be discouraged by the ruinous termination of an act, are the two maxims which, the wise say, from the principles of those who have investigated the subject

pope: Man's fitting work is known but by success achieved; In midst the plan revealed brings ruin ne'er to be retrieved
drewLazarus: So to perform an act as to publish it (only) at its termination is (true) manliness; for to announce it beforehand, will cause irremediable sorrow

pope: Easy to every man the speech that shows the way; Hard thing to shape one's life by words they say
drewLazarus: To say (how an act is to be performed) is (indeed) easy for any one; but far difficult it is to do according to what has been said
