pope: The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease
drewLazarus: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden

pope: Who easy access give to every man, they say, Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way
drewLazarus: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness

pope: Benevolence and high born dignity, These two are beaten paths of courtesy
drewLazarus: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all

pope: Men are not one because their members seem alike to outward view; Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true
drewLazarus: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract

pope: Of men of fruitful life, who kindly benefits dispense, The world unites to praise the 'noble excellence.'
drewLazarus: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity

pope: Contempt is evil though in sport They who man's nature know, E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show
drewLazarus: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated

pope: The world abides; for 'worthy' men its weight sustainWere it not so, 'twould fall to dust again
drewLazarus: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish

pope: Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, Whose souls are void of 'courtesy humane'
drewLazarus: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file

pope: Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail,'Tis uttermost disgrace in 'courtesy' to fail
drewLazarus: It is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful

pope: To him who knows not how to smile in kindly mirth, Darkness in daytime broods o'er all the vast and mighty earth
drewLazarus: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light

pope: Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured, Is ample wealth in churlish man's unopened coffers stored
drewLazarus: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the

pope: Who fills his house with ample store, enjoying none, Is dead Nought with the useless heap is done
drewLazarus: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him)

pope: Who giving nought, opines from wealth all blessing springs, Degraded birth that doting miser's folly brings
drewLazarus: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead miserly life will be born a demon

pope: Who lust to heap up wealth, but glory hold not dear, It burthens earth when on the stage of being they appear
drewLazarus: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame

pope: Whom no one loves, when he shall pass away, What doth he look to leave behind, I pray
drewLazarus: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one) regard as his own (in the world to come) ?

pope: Amid accumulated millions they are poor, Who nothing give and nought enjoy of all they store
drewLazarus: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches

pope: Their ample wealth is misery to men of churlish heart, Who nought themselves enjoy, and nought to worthy men impart
drewLazarus: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth

pope: Like woman fair in lonelihood who aged grows, Is wealth of him on needy men who nought bestows
drewLazarus: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband

pope: When he whom no man loves exults in great prosperity,'Tis as when fruits in midmost of the town some poisonous tree
drewLazarus: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town

pope: Who love abandon, self-afflict, and virtue's way forsakeTo heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take
drewLazarus: To heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take

pope: 'Tis as when rain cloud in the heaven grows day, When generous wealthy man endures brief poverty
drewLazarus: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while)

pope: To shrink abashed from evil deed is 'generous shame'; Other is that of bright-browed one of virtuous fame
drewLazarus: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids

pope: Food, clothing, and other things alike all beings own; By sense of shame the excellence of men is known
drewLazarus: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men but modesty is peculiar to the good

pope: All spirits homes of flesh as habitation claim, And perfect virtue ever dwells with shame
drewLazarus: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection

pope: And is not shame an ornament to men of dignity?Without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see
drewLazarus: Is not the modesty ornament of the noble ? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others)

pope: As home of virtuous shame by all the world the men are known, Who feel ashamed for others, guilt as for their own
drewLazarus: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fear his own and other's guilt

pope: Unless the hedge of shame inviolate remain, For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain
drewLazarus: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world

pope: The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make, But ne'er abandon virtuous shame for life's dear sake
drewLazarus: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life

pope: Though know'st no shame, while all around asha med must be:Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee
drewLazarus: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of

pope: 'Twill race consume if right observance fail;'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail
drewLazarus: Want of manners injures one's family; but want of modesty injures one's character

pope: 'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions, whenThose void of shame within hold intercourse with men
drewLazarus: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of puppet moved by a string

pope: Who says 'I'll do my work, nor slack my hand', His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand
drewLazarus: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family)

pope: The manly act and knowledge full, when these combineIn deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race's line
drewLazarus: One's family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances

pope: 'I'll make my race renowned,' if man shall say, With vest succinct the goddess leads the way
drewLazarus: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family

pope: Who labours for his race with unremitting pain, Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain
drewLazarus: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succeed

pope: With blameless life who seeks to build his race's fame, The world shall circle him, and kindred claim
drewLazarus: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means

pope: Of virtuous manliness the world accords the praiseTo him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise
drewLazarus: A man's true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family

pope: The fearless hero bears the brunt amid the warrior throng; Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong
drewLazarus: Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong

pope: Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear;'Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear
drewLazarus: As a family suffers by (one's) indolence and false dignity there is to be so season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family

pope: Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, Who would his household screen from every ill
drewLazarus: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil ?

pope: When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall, If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall
drewLazarus: If there are none to prop up and maintain a family (in distress), it will fall at the stroke of the axe of misfortune

pope: Howe'er they roam, the world must follow still the plougher's team; Though toilsome, culture of the ground as noblest toil esteem
drewLazarus: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent (form of labour); for people, though they go about (in search of various employments), have at last to resort to the farmer

pope: The ploughers are the linch-pin of the world; they bearThem up who other works perform, too weak its toils to share
drewLazarus: Agriculturists are (as it were) the linch-pin of the world for they support all other workers who cannot till the soil

pope: Who ploughing eat their food, they truly live:The rest to others bend subservient, eating what they give
drewLazarus: They alone live who live by agriculture; all others lead a cringing, dependent life

pope: O'er many a land they 'll see their monarch reign, Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain
drewLazarus: Patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king

pope: They nothing ask from others, but to askers give, Who raise with their own hands the food on which they live
drewLazarus: Those whose nature is to live by manual labour will never beg but give something to those who beg

pope: For those who 've left what all men love no place is found, When they with folded hands remain who till the ground
drewLazarus: If the farmer's hands are slackened, even the ascetic state will fail

pope: Reduce your soil to that dry state, When ounce is quarter-ounce's weight; Without one handful of manure, Abundant crops you thus secure
drewLazarus: If the land is dried so as to reduce one ounce of earth to a quarter, it will grow plentifully even without a handful of manure

pope: To cast manure is better than to plough; Weed well; to guard is more than watering now
drewLazarus: Manuring is better than ploughing; after weeding, watching is better than watering (it)

pope: When master from the field aloof hath stood; Then land will sulk, like wife in angry mood
drewLazarus: If the owner does not (personally) attend to his cultivation, his land will behave like an angry wife and yield him no pleasure

pope: The earth, that kindly dame, will laugh to see, Men seated idle pleading poverty
drewLazarus: The maiden, Earth, will laugh at the sight of those who plead poverty and lead an idle life

pope: You ask what sharper pain than poverty is known; Nothing pains more than poverty, save poverty alone
drewLazarus: There is nothing that afflicts (one) like poverty

pope: Malefactor matchless! poverty destroysThis world's and the next world's joys
drewLazarus: When cruel poverty comes on, it deprives one of both the present and future (bliss)

pope: Importunate desire, which poverty men name, Destroys both old descent and goodly fame
drewLazarus: Hankering poverty destroys at once the greatness of (one's) ancient descent and (the dignity of one's) speech

pope: From penury will spring, 'mid even those of noble race, Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace
drewLazarus: Even in those of high birth, poverty will produce the fault of uttering mean words

pope: From poverty, that grievous woe, Attendant sorrows plenteous grow
drewLazarus: The misery of poverty brings in its train many (more) miseries

pope: Though deepest sense, well understood, the poor man's words convey, Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away
drewLazarus: The words of the poor are profitless, though they may be sound in thought and clear in expression

pope: From indigence devoid of virtue's grace, The mother e'en that bare, estranged, will turn her face
drewLazarus: He that is reduced to absolute poverty will be regarded as a stranger even by his own mother

pope: And will it come today as yesterday, The grief of want that eats my soul away
drewLazarus: Is the poverty that almost killed me yesterday, to meet me today too ?

pope: Amid the flames sleep may men's eyelids close, In poverty the eye knows no repose
drewLazarus: One may sleep in the midst of fire; but by no means in the midst of poverty

pope: Unless the destitute will utterly themselves deny, They cause their neighbour's salt and vinegar to die
drewLazarus: The destitute poor, who do not renounce their bodies, only consume their neighbour's salt and water

pope: When those you find from whom 'tis meet to ask,- for aid apply; Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny
drewLazarus: If you meet with those that may be begged of, you may beg; (but) if they withhold (their gift) it is their blame and not yours

pope: Even to ask an alms may pleasure give, If what you ask without annoyance you receive
drewLazarus: Even begging may be pleasant, if what is begged for is obtained without grief (to him that begs)

pope: The men who nought deny, but know what's due, before their faceTo stand as suppliants affords especial grace
drewLazarus: There is even a beauty in standing before and begging of those who are liberal in their gifts and understand their duty (to beggars)

pope: Like giving alms, may even asking pleasant seem, From men who of denial never even dream
drewLazarus: To beg of such as never think of withholding (their charity) even in their dreams, is in fact the same as giving (it oneself);

pope: Because on earth the men exist, who never say them nay, Men bear to stand before their eyes for help to pray
drewLazarus: As there are in the world those that give without refusing, there are (also) those that prefer to beg by simply standing before them

pope: It those you find from evil of 'denial' free, At once all plague of poverty will flee
drewLazarus: All the evil of begging will be removed at the sight of those who are far from the evil of refusing

pope: If men are found who give and no harsh words of scorn employ, The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy
drewLazarus: Beggars rejoice exceedingly when they behold those who bestow (their alms) with kindness and courtesy

pope: If askers cease, the mighty earth, where cooling fountains flow, Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go
drewLazarus: If there were no beggars, (the actions done in) the cool wide world would only resemble the movement of a puppet

pope: What glory will there be to men of generous soul, When none are found to love the askers' role
drewLazarus: What (praise) would there be to givers (of alms) if there were no beggars to ask for and reveive (them)

pope: Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof; The plague of poverty itself is ample proof
drewLazarus: He who begs ought not to be angry (at a refusal); for even the misery of (his own) poverty should be a sufficient reason (for so doing)

pope: Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live, Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give
drewLazarus: Not to beg (at all) even from those excellent persons who cheerfully give without refusing, will do immense good

pope: If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go, Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so
drewLazarus: If the Creator of the world has decreed even begging as a means of livelihood, may he too go abegging and perish

pope: Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say,'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away.'
drewLazarus: There is no greater folly than the boldness with which one seeks to remedy the evils of poverty by begging (rather than by working)

pope: Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worthHas excellence of greatness that transcends the earth
drewLazarus: Even the whole world cannot sufficiently praise the dignity that would not beg even in the midst of destitution

pope: Nothing is sweeter than to taste the toil-won cheer, Though mess of pottage as tasteless as the water clear
drewLazarus: Even thin gruel is ambrosia to him who has obtained it by labour

pope: E'en if a draught of water for a cow you ask, Nought's so distasteful to the tongue as beggar's task
drewLazarus: There is nothing more disgraceful to one's tongue than to use it in begging water even for a cow

pope: One thing I beg of beggars all, 'If beg ye may, Of those who hide their wealth, beg not, I pray.'
drewLazarus: I beseech all beggars and say, "If you need to beg, never beg of those who give unwillingly."

pope: The fragile bark of beggaryWrecked on denial's rock will lie
drewLazarus: The unsafe raft of begging will split when it strikes on the rock of refusal

pope: The heart will melt away at thought of beggary, With thought of stern repulse 'twill perish utterly
drewLazarus: To think of (the evil of) begging is enough to melt one's heart; but to think of refusal is enough to break it

pope: E'en as he asks, the shamefaced asker dies; Where shall his spirit hide who help denies
drewLazarus: Saying "No" to a beggar takes away his life. (but as that very word will kill the refuser) where then would the latter's life hide itself ?

pope: The base resemble men in outward form, I ween; But counterpart exact to them I've never seen
drewLazarus: The base resemble men perfectly (as regards form); and we have not seen such (exact) resemblance (among any other species)

pope: Than those of grateful heart the base must luckier be, Their minds from every anxious thought are free
drewLazarus: The low enjoy more felicity than those who know what is good; for the former are not troubled with anxiety (as to the good)

pope: The base are as the Gods; they tooDo ever what they list to do
drewLazarus: The base resemble the Gods; for the base act as they like

pope: When base men those behold of conduct vile, They straight surpass them, and exulting smile
drewLazarus: The base feels proud when he sees persons whose acts meaner than his own

pope: Fear is the base man's virtue; if that fail, Intense desire some little may avail
drewLazarus: (The principle of) behaviour in the mean is chiefly fear; if not, hope of gain, to some extent

pope: The base are like the beaten drum; for, when they hearThe sound the secret out in every neighbour's ear
drewLazarus: The base are like a drum that is beaten, for they unburden to others the secrets they have heard

pope: From off their moistened hands no clinging grain they shake, Unless to those with clenched fist their jaws who break
drewLazarus: The mean will not (even) shake off (what sticks to) their hands (soon after a meal) to any but those who would break their jaws with their clenched fists

pope: The good to those will profit yield fair words who use; The base, like sugar-cane, will profit those who bruise
drewLazarus: The great bestow (their alms) as soon as they are informed; (but) the mean, like the sugar-cane, only when they are tortured to death

pope: If neighbours clothed and fed he see, the baseIs mighty man some hidden fault to trace
drewLazarus: The base will bring an evil (accusation) against others, as soon as he sees them (enjoying) good food

pope: For what is base man fit, if griefs assail?Himself to offer, there and then, for sale
drewLazarus: The base will hasten to sell themselves as soon as a calamity has befallen them. For what else are they fitted ?

pope: Goddess? or peafowl rare? She whose ears rich jewels wear, Is she a maid of human kind? All wildered is my mind
drewLazarus: Is this jewelled female a celestial, a choice peahen, or a human being ? My mind is perplexed

pope: She of the beaming eyes, To my rash look her glance replies, As if the matchless goddess' hand Led forth an armed band
drewLazarus: This female beauty returning my looks is like a celestial maiden coming with an army to contend against me

pope: Death's form I formerly Knew not; but now 'tis plain to me; He comes in lovely maiden's guise, With soul-subduing eyes
drewLazarus: I never knew before what is called Yama; I see it now; it is the eyes that carry on a great fight with (the help of) female qualities

pope: In sweet simplicity, A woman's gracious form hath she; But yet those eyes, that drink my life, Are with the form at strife
drewLazarus: These eyes that seem to kill those who look at them are as it were in hostilities with this feminine simplicity

pope: The light that on me gleams, Is it death's dart? or eye's bright beams?Or fawn's shy glance? All three appear In form of maiden here
drewLazarus: Is it Yama, (a pair of) eyes or a hind ?- Are not all these three in the looks of this maid ?

pope: If cruel eye-brow's bow, Unbent, would veil those glances now; The shafts that wound this trembling heart Her eyes no more would dart
drewLazarus: Her eyes will cause (me) no trembling sorrow, if they are properly hidden by her cruel arched eyebrows

pope: As veil o'er angry eyes Of raging elephant that lies, The silken cincture's folds invest This maiden's panting breast
drewLazarus: The cloth that covers the firm bosom of this maiden is (like) that which covers the eyes of a rutting elephant

pope: Ah woe is me my might, That awed my foemen in the fight, By lustre of that beaming brow Borne down, lies broken now
drewLazarus: On her bright brow alone is destroyed even that power of mine that used to terrify the most fearless

pope: Like tender fawn's her eye; Clothed on is she with modesty; What added beauty can be lent; By alien ornament
drewLazarus: Of what use are other jewels to her who is adorned with modesty, and the meek looks of a hind ?

pope: The palm-tree's fragrant wine, To those who taste yields joys divine; But love hath rare felicity For those that only see
drewLazarus: Unlike boiled honey which yields delight only when it is drunk, love gives pleasure even when looked at

pope: A double witchery have glances of her liquid eye; One glance is glance that brings me pain; the other heals again
drewLazarus: There are two looks in the dyed eyes of this (fair one); one causes pain, and the other is the cure thereof

pope: The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright, Is more than half of love's supreme delight
drewLazarus: A single stolen glance of her eyes is more than half the pleasure (of sexual embrace)

pope: She looked, and looking drooped her head:On springing shoot of love 'its water shed
drewLazarus: She has looked (at men) and stooped (her head); and that (sign) waters as it were (the corn of) our love

pope: I look on her: her eyes are on the ground the while:I look away: she looks on me with timid smile
drewLazarus: When I look, she looks down; when I do not, she looks and smiles gently

pope: She seemed to see me not; but yet the maidHer love, by smiling side-long glance, betrayed
drewLazarus: She not only avoids a direct look at me, but looks as it were with a half-closed eye and smiles

pope: Though with their lips affection they disown, Yet, when they hate us not, 'tis quickly known
drewLazarus: Though they may speak harshly as if they were strangers, the words of the friendly are soon understood

pope: The slighting words that anger feign, while eyes their love revealAre signs of those that love, but would their love conceal
drewLazarus: Little words that are harsh and looks that are hateful are (but) the expressions of lovers who wish to act like strangers

pope: I gaze, the tender maid relents the while; And, oh the matchless grace of that soft smile
drewLazarus: When I look, the pitying maid looks in return and smiles gently; and that is a comforting sign for me

pope: The look indifferent, that would its love disguise, Is only read aright by lovers' eyes
drewLazarus: Both the lovers are capable of looking at each other in an ordinary way, as if they were perfect strangers

pope: When eye to answering eye reveals the tale of love, All words that lips can say must useless prove
drewLazarus: The words of the mouths are of no use whatever, when there is perfect agreement between the eyes (of lovers)

pope: All joys that senses five- sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch- can give, In this resplendent armlets-bearing damsel live
drewLazarus: The (simultaneous) enjoyment of the five senses of sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch can only be found with bright braceleted (women)

pope: Disease and medicine antagonists we surely see; This maid, to pain she gives, herself is remedy
drewLazarus: The remedy for a disease is always something different (from it); but for the disease caused by this jewelled maid, she is herself the cure

pope: Than rest in her soft arms to whom the soul is giv'n, Is any sweeter joy in his, the Lotus-eyed-one's heaven
drewLazarus: Can the lotus-eyed Vishnu's heaven be indeed as sweet to those who delight to sleep in the delicate arms of their beloved ?

pope: Withdraw, it burns; approach, it soothes the pain; Whence did the maid this wondrous fire obtain
drewLazarus: From whence has she got this fire that burns when I withdraw and cools when I approach ?

pope: In her embrace, whose locks with flowery wreaths are bound, Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found
drewLazarus: Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found

pope: Ambrosia are the simple maiden's arms; when I attainTheir touch, my withered life puts forth its buds again
drewLazarus: The shoulders of this fair one are made of ambrosia, for they revive me with pleasure every time I embrace them

pope: As when one eats from household store, with kindly graceSharing his meal: such is this golden maid's embrace
drewLazarus: The embraces of a gold-complexioned beautiful female are as pleasant as to dwell in one's own house and live by one's own (earnings) after distributing (a portion of it in charity)

pope: Sweet is the strict embrace of those whom fond affection binds, Where no dissevering breath of discord entrance finds
drewLazarus: To ardent lovers sweet is the embrace that cannot be penetrated even by a breath of breeze

pope: The jealous variance, the healing of the strife, reunion gained:These are the fruits from wedded love obtained
drewLazarus: Love quarrel, reconciliation and intercourse - these are the advantages reaped by those who marry for lust

pope: The more men learn, the more their lack of learning they detect;'Tis so when I approach the maid with gleaming jewels decked
drewLazarus: As (one's) ignorance is discovered the more one learns, so does repeated intercourse with a welladorned female (only create a desire for more)

pope: O flower of the sensitive plant! than theeMore tender's the maiden beloved by me
drewLazarus: May you flourish, O Anicham! you have a delicate nature But my beloved is more delicate than you

pope: You deemed, as you saw the flowers, her eyes were as flowers, my soul, That many may see; it was surely some folly that over you stole
drewLazarus: O my soul, fancying that flowers which are seen by many can resemble her eyes, you become confused at the sight of them

pope: As tender shoot her frame; teeth, pearls; around her odours blend; Darts are the eyes of her whose shoulders like the bambu bend
drewLazarus: The complexion of this bamboo-shouldered one is that of a shoot; her teeth, are pearls; her breath,

pope: The lotus, seeing her, with head demiss, the ground would eye, And say, 'With eyes of her, rich gems who wears, we cannot vie.'
drewLazarus: If the blue lotus could see, it would stoop and look at the ground saying, "I can never resemble the eyes of this excellent jewelled one."

pope: The flowers of the sensitive plant as a girdle around her she placed; The stems she forgot to nip off; they 'll weigh down the delicate waist
drewLazarus: No merry drums will be beaten for the (tender) waist of her who has adorned herself with the anicham without having removed its stem

pope: The stars perplexed are rushing wildly from their spheres; For like another moon this maiden's face appears
drewLazarus: The stars have become confused in their places not being able to distinguish between the moon and the maid's countenance

pope: In moon, that waxing waning shines, as sports appear, Are any spots discerned in face of maiden here
drewLazarus: Could there be spots in the face of this maid like those in the bright full moon ?

pope: Farewell, O moon! If that thine orb could shineBright as her face, thou shouldst be love of mine
drewLazarus: If you can indeed shine like the face of women, flourish, O moon, for then would you be worth loving ?

pope: If as her face, whose eyes are flowers, thou wouldst have charms for me, Shine for my eyes alone, O moon, shine not for all to see
drewLazarus: O moon, if you wish to resemble the face of her whose eyes are like (these) flowers, do not appear so as to be seen by all

pope: The flower of the sensitive plant, and the down on the swan's white breast, As the thorn are harsh, by the delicate feet of this maiden pressed
drewLazarus: The anicham and the feathers of the swan are to the feet of females, like the fruit of the (thorny) Nerunji

pope: The dew on her white teeth, whose voice is soft and low, Is as when milk and honey mingled flow
drewLazarus: The water which oozes from the white teeth of this soft speeched damsel is like a mixture of milk and honey

pope: Between this maid and me the friendship kindIs as the bonds that soul and body bind
drewLazarus: The love between me and this damsel is like the union of body and soul

pope: For her with beauteous brow, the maid I love, there place is none; To give her image room, O pupil of mine eye, begone
drewLazarus: O you image in the pupil (of my eye)! depart; there is no room for (my) fair-browed beloved

pope: Life is she to my very soul when she draws nigh; Dissevered from the maid with jewels rare, I die
drewLazarus: My fair-jewelled one resembles the living soul (when she is in union with me), the dying soul when she leaves me

pope: I might recall, if I could once forget; but from my heartHer charms fade not, whose eyes gleam like the warrior's dart
drewLazarus: If I had forgotten her who has bright battling eyes, I would have remembered (thee); but I never forget her (Thus says he to her maid)

pope: My loved one's subtle form departs not from my eyes; I wink them not, lest I should pain him where he lies
drewLazarus: My lover would not depart from mine eyes; even if I wink, he would not suffer (from pain); he is so ethereal

pope: My love doth ever in my eyes reside; I stain them not, fearing his form to hide
drewLazarus: As my lover abides in my eyes, I will not even paint them, for he would (then) have to conceal himself

pope: Within my heart my lover dwells; from food I turnThat smacks of heat, lest he should feel it burn
drewLazarus: As my lover is in my heart, I am afraid of eating (anything) hot, for I know it would pain him

pope: I fear his form to hide, nor close my eyes:'Her love estranged is gone!' the village cries
drewLazarus: I will not wink, knowing that if I did, my lover would hide himself; and for this reason, this town says, he is unloving

pope: Rejoicing in my very soul he ever lies;'Her love estranged is gone far off!' the village cries
drewLazarus: My lover dwells in my heart with perpetual delight; but the town says he is unloving and (therefore) dwells afar

pope: To those who 've proved love's joy, and now afflicted mourn, Except the helpful 'horse of palm', no other strength remains
drewLazarus: To those who after enjoyment of sexual pleasure suffer (for want of more), there is no help so efficient as the palmyra horse

pope: My body and my soul, that can no more endure, Will lay reserve aside, and mount the 'horse of palm'
drewLazarus: Having got rid of shame, the suffering body and soul save themselves on the palmyra horse

pope: I once retained reserve and seemly manliness; To-day I nought possess but lovers' 'horse of palm'
drewLazarus: Modesty and manliness were once my own; now, my own is the palmyra horse that is ridden by the lustful

pope: Love's rushing tide will sweep away the raftOf seemly manliness and shame combined
drewLazarus: The raft of modesty and manliness, is, alas, carried-off by the strong current of lust

pope: The maid that slender armlets wears, like flowers entwined, Has brought me 'horse of palm,' and pangs of eventide
drewLazarus: She with the small garland-like bracelets has given me the palmyra horse and the sorrow that is endured at night

pope: Of climbing 'horse of palm' in midnight hour, I think; My eyes know no repose for that same simple maid
drewLazarus: Mine eyes will not close in sleep on your mistress's account; even at midnight will I think of mounting the palmyra horse

pope: There's nought of greater worth than woman's long-enduring soul, Who, vexed by love like ocean waves, climbs not the 'horse of palm'
drewLazarus: There is nothing so noble as the womanly nature that would not ride the palmyra horse, though plunged a sea of lust

pope: In virtue hard to move, yet very tender, too, are we; Love deems not so, would rend the veil, and court publicity
drewLazarus: Even the Lust (of women) transgresses its secrecy and appears in public, forgetting that they are too chaste and liberal (to be overcome by it)

pope: 'There's no one knows my heart,' so says my love, And thus, in public ways, perturbed will rove
drewLazarus: And thus, in public ways, perturbed will rove

pope: Before my eyes the foolish make a mock of me, Because they ne'er endured the pangs I now must drie
drewLazarus: Even strangers laugh (at us) so as to be seen by us, for they have not suffered

pope: By this same rumour's rise, my precious life stands fast; Good fortune grant the many know this not
drewLazarus: My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour, and this, to my good luck no others are aware of

pope: The village hath to us this rumour giv'n, that makes her mine; Unweeting all the rareness of the maid with flower-like eyne
drewLazarus: Not knowing the value of her whose eyes are like flowers this town has got up a rumour about me

pope: The rumour spread within the town, is it not gain to me?It is as though that were obtained that may not be
drewLazarus: Will I not get a rumour that is known to the (whole) town ? For what I have not got is as if I had got it (already)

pope: The rumour rising makes my love to rise; My love would lose its power and languish otherwise
drewLazarus: Rumour increases the violence of my passion; without it it would grow weak and waste away

pope: The more man drinks, the more he ever drunk would be; The more my love's revealed, the sweeter 'tis to me
drewLazarus: As drinking liquor is delightful (to one) whenever one is in mirth, so is lust delightful to me whenever it is the subject of rumour

pope: I saw him but one single day: rumour spreads soonAs darkness, when the dragon seizes on the moon
drewLazarus: It was but a single day that I looked on (my lover); but the rumour thereof has spread like the seizure of the moon by the serpent

pope: My anguish grows apace: the town's reportManures it; my mother's word doth water it
drewLazarus: This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women and watered by the (harsh) words of my mother

pope: With butter-oil extinguish fire! 'Twill proveHarder by scandal to extinguish love
drewLazarus: To say that one could extinguish passion by rumour is like extinguishing fire with ghee

pope: When he who said 'Fear not!' hath left me blamed, While many shrink, can I from rumour hide ashamed
drewLazarus: When the departure of him who said "fear not" has put me to shame before others, why need I be ashamed of scandal

pope: If we desire, who loves will grant what we require; This town sends forth the rumour we desire
drewLazarus: The rumour I desire is raised by the town (itself); and my lover would if desired consent (to my following him)

pope: If you will say, 'I leave thee not,' then tell me so; Of quick return tell those that can survive this woe
drewLazarus: If it is not departure, tell me; but if it is your speedy return, tell it to those who would be alive then

pope: It once was perfect joy to look upon his face; But now the fear of parting saddens each embrace
drewLazarus: His very look was once pleasing; but (now) even intercourse is painful through fear of separation

pope: To trust henceforth is hard, if ever he depart, E'en he, who knows his promise and my breaking heart
drewLazarus: As even the lover who understands (everything) may at times depart, confidence is hardly possible

pope: If he depart, who fondly said, 'Fear not,' what blame's incurredBy those who trusted to his reassuring word
drewLazarus: If he who bestowed his love and said "fear not" should depart, will it be the fault of those who believed in (his) assuring words ?

pope: If you would guard my life, from going him restrainWho fills my life! If he depart, hardly we meet again
drewLazarus: If you would save (my life), delay the departure of my destined (husband); for if he departs, intercourse will become impossible

pope: To cherish longing hope that he should ever gracious be, Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me
drewLazarus: Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me

pope: The bracelet slipping from my wrist announced beforeDeparture of the Prince that rules the ocean shore
drewLazarus: Do not the rings that begin to slide down my fingers forebode the separation of my lord ?

pope: 'Tis sad to sojourn in the town where no kind kinsmen dwell;'Tis sadder still to bid a friend beloved farewell
drewLazarus: Painful is it to live in a friendless town; but far more painful is it to part from one's lover

pope: Fire burns the hands that touch; but smart of loveWill burn in hearts that far away remove
drewLazarus: Fire burns when touched; but, like the sickness of love, can it also burn when removed ?

pope: Sorrow's sadness meek sustaining, Driving sore distress away, Separation uncomplaining Many bear the livelong day
drewLazarus: As if there were many indeed that can consent to the impossible, kill their pain, endure separation and yet continue to live afterwards

pope: I would my pain conceal, but see! it surging swells, As streams to those that draw from ever-springing wells
drewLazarus: I would hide this pain from others; but it (only) swells like a spring to those who drain it

pope: I cannot hide this pain of mine, yet shame restrainsWhen I would tell it out to him who caused my pains
drewLazarus: I cannot conceal this pain, nor can I relate it without shame to him who has caused it

pope: My soul, like porter's pole, within my wearied frame, Sustains a two-fold burthen poised, of love and shame
drewLazarus: (Both) lust and shame, with my soul for their shoulder pole balance themselves on a body that cannot bear them

pope: A sea of love, 'tis true, I see stretched out before, But not the trusty bark that wafts to yonder shore
drewLazarus: There is indeed a flood of lust; but there is no raft of safety to cross it with

pope: Who work us woe in friendship's trustful hour, What will they prove when angry tempests lower
drewLazarus: What will they prove when angry tempests lower?

pope: A happy love 's sea of joy; but mightier sorrows rollFrom unpropitious love athwart the troubled soul
drewLazarus: The pleasure of lust is (as great as) the sea; but the pain of lust is far greater

pope: I swim the cruel tide of love, and can no shore descry, In watches of the night, too, 'mid the waters, only I
drewLazarus: I have swam across the terrible flood of lust, but have not seen its shore; even at midnight I am alone; still I live

pope: All living souls in slumber soft she steeps; But me alone kind night for her companing keeps
drewLazarus: The night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures, has me alone for her companion

pope: More cruel than the cruelty of him, the cruel one, In these sad times are lengthening hours of night I watch alone
drewLazarus: The long nights of these days are far more cruel than the heartless one who is torturing me

pope: When eye of mine would as my soul go forth to him, It knows not how through floods of its own tears to swim
drewLazarus: Could mine eyes travel like my thoughts to the abode (of my absent lord), they would not swim in this flood of tears

pope: They showed me him, and then my endless painI saw: why then should weeping eyes complain
drewLazarus: As this incurable malady has been caused by my eyes which showed (him) to me, why should they now weep for (him)

pope: How glancing eyes, that rash unweeting looked that day, With sorrow measureless are wasting now away
drewLazarus: The dyed eyes that (then) looked without foresight, why should they now endure sorrow, without feeling sharply (their own fault)

pope: The eyes that threw such eager glances round erewhileAre weeping now. Such folly surely claims a smile
drewLazarus: They themselves looked eagerly (on him) and now they weep. Is not this to be laughed at ?

pope: Those eyes have wept till all the fount of tears is dry, That brought upon me pain that knows no remedy
drewLazarus: These painted eyes have caused me a lasting mortal disease; and now they can weep no more, the tears having dried up

pope: The eye that wrought me more than sea could hold of woes, Is suffering pangs that banish all repose
drewLazarus: Mine eyes have caused me a lust that is greater than the sea and (they themselves) endure the torture of sleeplessness

pope: Oho! how sweet a thing to see! the eyeThat wrought this pain, in the same gulf doth lie
drewLazarus: The eyes that have given me this disease have themselves been seized with this (suffering) Oh! I am much delighted

pope: Aching, aching, let those exhaust their stream, That melting, melting, that day gazed on him
drewLazarus: The eyes that became tender and gazed intently on him, may they suffer so much as to dry up the fountain of their tears

pope: Who loved me once, onloving now doth here remain; Not seeing him, my eye no rest can gain
drewLazarus: He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him

pope: When he comes not, all slumber flies; no sleep when he is there; Thus every way my eyes have troubles hard to bear
drewLazarus: When he is away they do not sleep; when he is present they do not sleep; in either case, mine eyes endure unbearable agony

pope: It is not hard for all the town the knowledge to obtain, When eyes, as mine, like beaten tambours, make the mystery plain
drewLazarus: It is not difficult for the people of this place to understand the secret of those whose eyes, like mine, are as it were beaten drums

pope: I willed my lover absent should remain; Of pining's sickly hue to whom shall I complain
drewLazarus: I who (then) consented to the absence of my loving lord, to whom can I (now) relate the fact of my having turned sallow

pope: 'He gave': this sickly hue thus proudly speaks, Then climbs, and all my frame its chariot makes
drewLazarus: Sallowness, as if proud of having been caused by him, would now ride on my person

pope: Of comeliness and shame he me bereft, While pain and sickly hue, in recompense, he left
drewLazarus: He has taken (away) my beauty and modesty, and given me instead disease and sallowness

pope: I meditate his words, his worth is theme of all I say, This sickly hue is false that would my trust betray
drewLazarus: I think (of him); and what I speak about is but his excellence; still is there sallowness; and this is deceitful

pope: My lover there went forth to roam; This pallor of my frame usurps his place at home
drewLazarus: Just as my lover departed then, did not sallowness spread here on my person ?

pope: As darkness waits till lamp expires, to fill the place, This pallor waits till I enjoy no more my lord's embrace
drewLazarus: Just as darkness waits for the failing light; so does sallowness wait for the laxity of my husband's intercourse

pope: I lay in his embrace, I turned unwittingly; Forthwith this hue, as you might grasp it, came on me
drewLazarus: I who was in close embrace just turned aside and the moment I did so, sallowness came on me like something to be seized on

pope: On me, because I pine, they cast a slur; But no one says, 'He first deserted her.'
drewLazarus: Besides those who say "she has turned sallow" there are none who say "he has forsaken her"

pope: Well let my frame, as now, be sicklied o'er with pain, If he who won my heart's consent, in good estate remain
drewLazarus: If he is clear of guilt who has conciliated me (to his departure) let my body suffer its due and turn sallow

pope: 'Tis well, though men deride me for my sickly hue of pain; If they from calling him unkind, who won my love, refrain
drewLazarus: It would be good to be said of me that I have turned sallow, if friends do not reproach with unkindness him who pleased me (then)

pope: The bliss to be beloved by those they love who gains, Of love the stoneless, luscious fruit obtains
drewLazarus: The women who are beloved by those whom they love, have they have not got the stone-less fruit of sexual delight ?

pope: As heaven on living men showers blessings from above, Is tender grace by lovers shown to those they love
drewLazarus: The bestowal of love by the beloved on those who love them is like the rain raining (at the proper season) on those who live by it

pope: Who love and are beloved to them aloneBelongs the boast, 'We've made life's very joys our own.'
drewLazarus: The pride that says "we shall live" suits only those who are loved by their beloved (husbands)

pope: Those well-beloved will luckless prove, Unless beloved by those they love
drewLazarus: Even those who are esteemed (by other women) are devoid of excellence, if they are not loved by their beloved

pope: From him I love to me what gain can be, Unless, as I love him, he loveth me
drewLazarus: He who is beloved by me, what will he do to me, if I am not beloved by him ?

pope: Love on one side is bad; like balanced loadBy porter borne, love on both sides is good
drewLazarus: Lust, like the weight of the KAVADI, pains if it lies in one end only but pleases if it is in both

pope: While Kaman rushes straight at me alone, Is all my pain and wasting grief unknown
drewLazarus: Would not cupid who abides and contends in one party (only) witness the pain and sorrow (in that party)?

pope: Who hear from lover's lips no pleasant word from day to day, Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they
drewLazarus: There is no one in the world so hard-hearted as those who can live without receiving (even) a kind word from their beloved

pope: Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me, Yet every accent of his voice is melody
drewLazarus: Though my beloved bestows no love on one, still are his words sweet to my ears

pope: Tell him thy pain that loves not thee?Farewell, my soul, fill up the sea
drewLazarus: Live, O my soul, would you who relate your great sorrow to strangers, try rather to fill up your own sea (of sorrow)

pope: From thought of her unfailing gladness springs, Sweeter than palm-rice wine the joy love brings
drewLazarus: Sexuality is sweeter than liquor, because when remembered, it creates a most rapturous delight

pope: How great is love! Behold its sweetness past belief!Think on the lover, and the spirit knows no grief
drewLazarus: Even to think of one's beloved gives one no pain Sexuality, in any degree, is always delightful

pope: A fit of sneezing threatened, but it passed away; He seemed to think of me, but do his fancies stray
drewLazarus: I feel as if I am going to sneeze but do not, and (therefore) my beloved is about to think (of me) but does not

pope: Have I a place within his heart!From mine, alas! he never doth depart
drewLazarus: He continues to abide in my soul, do I likewise abide in his ?

pope: Me from his heart he jealously excludes:Hath he no shame who ceaseless on my heart intrudes
drewLazarus: He who has imprisoned me in his soul, is he ashamed to enter incessantly into mine

pope: How live I yet? I live to ponder o'erThe days of bliss with him that are no more
drewLazarus: I live by remembering my (former) intercourse with him; if it were not so, how could I live ?

pope: If I remembered not what were I then? And yet, The fiery smart of what my spirit knows not to forget
drewLazarus: I have never forgotten (the pleasure); even to think of it burns my soul; could I live, if I should ever forget it ?

pope: My frequent thought no wrath excites It is not so?This honour doth my love on me bestow
drewLazarus: He will not be angry however much I may think of him; is it not so much the delight my beloved

pope: Dear life departs, when his ungracious deeds I ponder o'er, Who said erewhile, 'We're one for evermore'
drewLazarus: My precious life is wasting away by thinking too much on the cruelty of him who said we were not different

pope: Set not; so may'st thou prosper, moon! that eyes may seeMy love who went away, but ever bides with me
drewLazarus: May you live, O Moon! Do not set, that I mine see him who has departed without quitting my soul

pope: It came and brought to me, that nightly vision rare, A message from my love,- what feast shall I prepare
drewLazarus: Where with shall I feast the dream which has brought me my dear one's messenger ?

pope: If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore, The tale of my long-suffering life I'll tell my loved one o'er
drewLazarus: If my fish-like painted eyes should, at my begging, close in sleep, I could fully relate my sufferings to my lord

pope: Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows, In dreams I see; and so my lifetime goes
drewLazarus: My life lasts because in my dream I behold him who does not favour me in my waking hours

pope: Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not meIn waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see
drewLazarus: There is pleasure in my dream, because in it I seek and obtain him who does not visit me in my wakefulness

pope: As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet, So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet
drewLazarus: I saw him in my waking hours, and then it was pleasant; I see him just now in my dream, and it is (equally) pleasant

pope: And if there were no waking hour, my loveIn dreams would never from my side remove
drewLazarus: Were there no such thing as wakefulness, my beloved (who visited me) in my dream would not depart from me

pope: The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems, Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams
drewLazarus: The cruel one who would not favour me in my wakefulness, what right has he to torture me in my dreams?

pope: And when I sleep he holds my form embraced; And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste
drewLazarus: When I am asleep he rests on my shoulders, (but) when I awake he hastens into my soul

pope: In dreams who ne'er their lover's form perceive, For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve
drewLazarus: They who have no dear ones to behold in their dreams blame him who visits me not in my waking hours

pope: They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone; In dreams they surely see him not,- these people of the town;
drewLazarus: The women of this place say he has forsaken me in my wakefulness I think they have not seen him visit me in my dreams

pope: Thou art not evening, but a spear that doth devourThe souls of brides; farewell, thou evening hour
drewLazarus: Live, O you evening are you (the former) evening? No, you are the season that slays (married) women

pope: Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide!Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride
drewLazarus: A long life to you, O dark evening! You are sightless Is your help-mate (also) as hard-hearted as mine

pope: With buds of chilly dew wan evening's shade enclose; My anguish buds space and all my sorrow grows
drewLazarus: The evening that (once) came in with trembling and dimness (now) brings me an aversion for life and increasing sorrow

pope: When absent is my love, the evening hour descends, As when an alien host to field of battle wends
drewLazarus: In the absence of my lover, evening comes in like slayers on the field of slaughter

pope: O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring'st reliefO eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief
drewLazarus: O eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief

pope: The pangs that evening brings I never knew, Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew
drewLazarus: Previous to my husband's departure, I know not the painful nature of evening

pope: My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower, Full-blown expands in evening hour
drewLazarus: This malady buds forth in the morning, expands all day long and blossoms in the evening

pope: The shepherd's pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear, For it proclaims the hour of ev'ning's fiery anguish near
drewLazarus: The shepherd's flute now sounds as a fiery forerunner of night, and is become a weapon that slays (me)

pope: If evening's shades, that darken all my soul, extend; From this afflicted town will would of grief ascend
drewLazarus: When night comes on confusing (everyone's) mind, the (whole) town will lose its sense and be plunged in sorrow

pope: This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly; Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me
drewLazarus: My (hitherto) unextinguished life is now lost in this bewildering night at the thought of him who has the nature of wealth

pope: Thine eyes grown dim are now ashamed the fragrant flow'rs to see, Thinking on him, who wand'ring far, leaves us in misery
drewLazarus: While we endure the unbearable sorrow, your eyes weep for him who is gone afar, and shun (the sight of) fragrant flowers

pope: The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears, As witness of the lover's lack of love appears
drewLazarus: The discoloured eyes that shed tears profusely seem to betray the unkindness of our beloved

pope: These withered arms, desertion's pangs abundantly display, That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day
drewLazarus: The shoulders that swelled on the day of our union (now) seem to announce our separation clearly (to the public)

pope: When lover went, then faded all their wonted charms, And armlets' golden round slips off from these poor wasted arms
drewLazarus: In the absence of your consort, your shoulders having lost their former beauty and fulness, your bracelets of pure gold have become loose

pope: These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone, The cruelty declare of that most cruel one
drewLazarus: The (loosened) bracelets, and the shoulders from which the old beauty has faded, relate the cruelty of the pitiless one

pope: I grieve, 'tis pain to me to hear him cruel chid, Because the armlet from my wasted arm has slid
drewLazarus: I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man, just because your shoulders are reduced and your bracelets loosened

pope: My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain, If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain
drewLazarus: Can you O my soul! gain glory by relating to the (so-called) cruel one the clamour of my fading shoulders?

pope: One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked, Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked
drewLazarus: When I once loosened the arms that were in embrace, the forehead of the gold-braceleted women turned sallow

pope: As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there; The maid's large liquid eyes were dimmed with care
drewLazarus: When but a breath of breeze penetrated our embrace, her large cool eyes became sallow

pope: The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now, Beholding what was done by that bright brow
drewLazarus: Was it at the sight of what the bright forehead had done that the sallowness of her eyes became sad?

pope: My heart, canst thou not thinking of some med'cine tell, Not any one, to drive away this grief incurable
drewLazarus: O my soul, will you not think and tell me some medicine be it what it may, that can cure this incurable malady?

pope: Since he loves not, thy smartIs folly, fare thee well my heart
drewLazarus: Is folly, fare thee well my heart!

pope: What comes of sitting here in pining thought, O heart? He knowsNo pitying thought, the cause of all these wasting woes
drewLazarus: O my soul! why remain (here) and suffer thinking (of him)? There are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him who has caused you this disease of sorrow

pope: O rid me of these eyes, my heart; for they, Longing to see him, wear my life away
drewLazarus: O my soul! take my eyes also with you, (if not), these would eat me up (in their desire) to see him

pope: O heart, as a foe, can I abandon utterlyHim who, though I long for him, longs not for me
drewLazarus: O my soul! can he who loves not though he is beloved, be forsaken saying he hates me (now)?

pope: My heart, false is the fire that burns; thou canst not wrath maintain, If thou thy love behold, embracing, soothing all thy pain
drewLazarus: O my soul! when you see the dear one who remove dislike by intercourse, you are displeased and continue to be so Nay, your displeasure is (simply) false

pope: Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart; For me, I cannot bear them both, my worthy heart
drewLazarus: O my good soul, give up either lust or honour, as for me I can endure neither

pope: Thou art befooled, my heart, thou followest him who flees from thee; And still thou yearning criest: 'He will nor pity show nor love to me.'
drewLazarus: You are a fool, O my soul! to go after my departed one, while you mourn that he is not kind enough to favour you

pope: My heart! my lover lives within my mind; Roaming, whom dost thou think to find
drewLazarus: O my soul! to whom would you repair, while the dear one is within yourself?

pope: If I should keep in mind the man who utterly renounces me, My soul must suffer further loss of dignity
drewLazarus: If I retain in my heart him who has left me without befriending me, I shall lose even the (inward) beauty that remains

pope: Of womanly reserve love's axe breaks through the door, Barred by the bolt of shame before
drewLazarus: The axe of lust can break the door of chastity which is bolted with the bolt of modesty

pope: What men call love is the one thing of merciless power; It gives my soul no rest, e'en in the midnight hour
drewLazarus: Even at midnight is my mind worried by lust, and this one thing, alas! is without mercy

pope: I would my love conceal, but like a sneezeIt shows itself, and gives no warning sign
drewLazarus: I would conceal my lust, but alas, it yields not to my will but breaks out like a sneeze

pope: In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail; But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil
drewLazarus: I say I would be firm, but alas, my malady breaks out from its concealment and appears in public

pope: The dignity that seeks not him who acts as foe, Is the one thing that loving heart can never know
drewLazarus: The dignity that would not go after an absent lover is not known to those who are sticken by love

pope: My grief how full of grace, I pray you see!It seeks to follow him that hateth me
drewLazarus: The sorrow I have endured by desiring to go after my absent lover, in what way is it excellent?

pope: No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove, When he returns my longing heart to bless with love
drewLazarus: I know nothing like shame when my beloved does from love (just) what is desired (by me)

pope: The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art, Are instruments that break through every guard of woman's heart
drewLazarus: Are not the enticing words of my trick-abounding roguish lover the weapon that breaks away my feminine firmness?

pope: 'I 'll shun his greeting'; saying thus with pride away I went:I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent
drewLazarus: I said I would feign dislike and so went (away); (but) I embraced him the moment I say my mind began to unite with him!

pope: 'We 'll stand aloof and then embrace': is this for them to say, Whose hearts are as the fat that in the blaze dissolves away
drewLazarus: Is it possible for those whose hearts melt like fat in the fire to say they can feign a strong dislike and remain so?

pope: My eyes have lost their brightness, sight is dimmed; my fingers worn, With nothing on the wall the days since I was left forlorn
drewLazarus: My finger has worn away by marking (on the wall) the days he has been absent while my eyes have lost their lustre and begin to fail

pope: O thou with gleaming jewels decked, could I forget for this one day, Henceforth these bracelets from my arms will slip, my beauty worn away
drewLazarus: O you bright-jewelled maid, if I forget (him) today, my shoulders will lose their beauty even in the other life and make my bracelets loose

pope: On victory intent, His mind sole company he went; And I yet life sustain And long to see his face again
drewLazarus: I still live by longing for the arrival of him who has gone out of love for victory and with valour as his guide

pope: 'He comes again, who left my side, and I shall taste love's joy,'-My heart with rapture swells, when thoughts like these my mind employ
drewLazarus: My heart is rid of its sorrow and swells with rapture to think of my absent lover returning with his love

pope: O let me see my spouse again and sate these longing eyes!That instant from my wasted frame all pallor flies
drewLazarus: May I look on my lover till I am satisfied and thereafter will vanish the sallowness of my slender shoulders

pope: O let my spouse but come again to me one day!I'll drink that nectar: wasting grief shall flee away
drewLazarus: May my husband return some day; and then will I enjoy (him) so as to destroy all this agonizing sorrow

pope: Shall I draw back, or yield myself, or shall both mingled be, When he returns, my spouse, dear as these eyes to me
drewLazarus: On the return of him who is as dear as my eyes, am I displeased or am I to embrace (him); or am I to do both?

pope: O would my king would fight, o'ercome, devide the spoil; At home, to-night, the banquet spread should crown the toil
drewLazarus: Let the king fight and gain (victories); (but) let me be united to my wife and feast the evening

pope: One day will seem like seven to those who watch and yearnFor that glad day when wanderers from afar return
drewLazarus: To those who suffer waiting for the day of return of their distant lovers one day is as long as seven days

pope: What's my return, the meeting hour, the wished-for greeting worth, If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth
drewLazarus: After (my wife) has died of a broken heart, what good will there be if she is to receive me, has received me, or has even embraced me?

pope: Thou hid'st it, yet thine eye, disdaining all restraint, Something, I know not, what, would utter of complaint
drewLazarus: Though you would conceal (your feelings), your painted eyes would not, for, transgressing (their bounds), they tell (me) something

pope: The simple one whose beauty fills mine eye, whose shoulders curveLike bambu stem, hath all a woman's modest sweet reserve
drewLazarus: Unusually great is the female simplicity of your maid whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders resemble the bamboo

pope: As through the crystal beads is seen the thread on which they 're strungSo in her beauty gleams some thought cannot find a tongue
drewLazarus: There is something that is implied in the beauty of this woman, like the thread that is visible in a garland of gems

pope: As fragrance in the opening bud, some secret liesConcealed in budding smile of this dear damsel's eyes
drewLazarus: There is something in the unmatured smile of this maid like the fragrance that is contained in an unblossomed bud

pope: The secret wiles of her with thronging armlets decked, Are medicines by which my raising grief is checked
drewLazarus: The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting contains a remedy that can cure my great sorrow

pope: While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved:It makes me think that I again shall live of love bereaved
drewLazarus: The embrace that fills me with comfort and gladness is capable of enduring (my former) sorrow and meditating on his want of love

pope: My severance from the lord of this cool shore, My very armlets told me long before
drewLazarus: My bracelets have understood before me the (mental) separation of him who rules the cool seashore

pope: My loved one left me, was it yesterday?Days seven my pallid body wastes away
drewLazarus: It was but yesterday my lover departed (from me); and it is seven days since my complexion turned sallow

pope: She viewed her tender arms, she viewed the armlets from them slid; She viewed her feet: all this the lady did
drewLazarus: She looked at her bracelets, her tender shoulders, and her feet; this was what she did there (significantly)

pope: To show by eye the pain of love, and for relief to pray, Is womanhood's most womanly device, men say
drewLazarus: To express their love-sickness by their eyes and resort to begging bespeaks more than ordinary female excellence

pope: Gladness at the thought, rejoicing at the sight, Not palm-tree wine, but love, yields such delight
drewLazarus: To please by thought and cheer by sight is peculiar, not to liquor but lust

pope: When as palmyra tall, fulness of perfect love we gain, Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain
drewLazarus: If women have a lust that exceeds even the measure of the palmyra fruit, they will not desire (to feign) dislike even as much as the millet

pope: Although his will his only law, he lightly value me, My heart knows no repose unless my lord I see
drewLazarus: Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband, still will they not be satisfied unless they see him

pope: My friend, I went prepared to show a cool disdain; My heart, forgetting all, could not its love restrain
drewLazarus: My heart, forgetting all, could not its love restrain

pope: The eye sees not the rod that paints it; nor can ISee any fault, when I behold my husband nigh
drewLazarus: Like the eyes which see not the pencil that paints it, I cannot see my husband's fault (just) when I meet him

pope: When him I see, to all his faults I 'm blind; But when I see him not, nothing but faults I find
drewLazarus: When I see my husband, I do not see any faults; but when I do not see him, I do not see anything but faults

pope: As those of rescue sure, who plunge into the stream, So did I anger feign, though it must falsehood seem
drewLazarus: Like those who leap into a stream which they know will carry them off, why should a wife feign dislike which she knows cannot hold out long?

pope: Though shameful ill it works, dear is the palm-tree wineTo drunkards; traitor, so to me that breast of thine
drewLazarus: O you rogue! your breast is to me what liquor is to those who rejoice in it, though it only gives them an unpleasant disgrace

pope: Love is tender as an opening flower In season dueTo gain its perfect bliss is rapture known to few
drewLazarus: Sexual delight is more delicate than a flower, and few are those who understand its real nature

pope: Her eye, as I drew nigh one day, with anger shone:By love o'erpowered, her tenderness surpassed my own
drewLazarus: She once feigned dislike in her eyes, but the warmth of her embrace exceeded my own

pope: You see his heart is his aloneO heart, why not be all my own
drewLazarus: O my soul! although you have seen how his soul stands by him, how is it you do not stand by me?

pope: 'Tis plain, my heart, that he 's estranged from thee; Why go to him as though he were not enemy
drewLazarus: O my soul! although you have known him who does not love me, still do you go to him, saying "he will not be displeased."

pope: 'The ruined have no friends, 'they say; and so, my heart, To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart
drewLazarus: O my soul! do you follow him at pleasure under the belief that the ruined have no friends?

pope: 'See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit,' I bade; Henceforth such council who will share with thee my heart
drewLazarus: O my soul! you would not first seem sulky and then enjoy (him); who then would in future consult you about such things?

pope: I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain; And thus my heart endures unceasing pain
drewLazarus: My soul fears when it is without him; it also fears when it is with him; it is subject to incessant sorrow

pope: My heart consumes me when I ponder lone, And all my lover's cruelty bemoan
drewLazarus: My mind has been (here) in order to eat me up (as it were) whenever I think of him in my solitude

pope: Fall'n 'neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart, Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame
drewLazarus: I have even forgotten my modesty, having been caught in my foolish mind which is not dignified enough to forget him

pope: If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore; My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o'er
drewLazarus: My soul which clings to life thinks only of his (own) gain in the belief that it would be disgraceful for it to despise him

pope: And who will aid me in my hour of grief, If my own heart comes not to my relief
drewLazarus: Who would help me out of one's distress, when one's own soul refuses help to one?

pope: A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown, When our own heart itself is not our own
drewLazarus: It is hardly possible for strangers to behave like relations, when one's own soul acts like a stranger

pope: Be still reserved, decline his profferred love; A little while his sore distress we 'll prove
drewLazarus: Let us witness awhile his keen suffering; just feign dislike and embrace him not

pope: A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess, Too long maintained, 'tis like the salt's excess
drewLazarus: A little dislike is like salt in proportion; to prolong it a little is like salt a little too much

pope: 'Tis heaping griefs on those whose hearts are grieved; To leave the grieving one without a fond embrace
drewLazarus: For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony

pope: To use no kind conciliating art when lover grieves, Is cutting out the root of tender winding plant that droops
drewLazarus: Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root

pope: Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulanceOf wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace
drewLazarus: An increased shyness in those whose eyes are like flowers is beautiful even to good and virtuous husbands

pope: Love without hatred is ripened fruit; Without some lesser strife, fruit immature
drewLazarus: Sexual pleasure, without prolonged and short-lived dislike, is like too ripe, and unripe fruit

pope: A lovers' quarrel brings its pain, when mind afraidAsks doubtful, 'Will reunion sweet be long delayed?'
drewLazarus: The doubt as to whether intercourse would take place soon or not, creates a sorrow (even) in feigned dislike

pope: What good can grieving do, when none who loveAre there to know the grief thy soul endures
drewLazarus: What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow?

pope: Water is pleasant in the cooling shade; So coolness for a time with those we love
drewLazarus: Like water in the shade, dislike is delicious only in those who love

pope: Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing, To think within my heart with love is fond desire
drewLazarus: It is nothing but strong desire that makes her mind unite with me who can leave her to her own dislike

pope: From thy regard all womankind Enjoys an equal grace; O thou of wandering fickle mind, I shrink from thine embrace
drewLazarus: You are given to prostitution; all those who are born as womankind enjoy you with their eyes in an ordinary way I will not embrace you

pope: One day we silent sulked; he sneezed: The reason well I knew; He thought that I, to speak well pleased, Would say, 'Long life to you!'
drewLazarus: When I continued to be sulky he sneezed and thought I would (then) wish him a long life

pope: I wreathed with flowers one day my brow, The angry tempest lowers; She cries, 'Pray, for what woman now Do you put on your flowers?'
drewLazarus: Even if I were adorned with a garland of branch-flowers, she would say I did so to show it to another woman

pope: 'I love you more than all beside,' 'T was thus I gently spoke;'What all, what all?' she instant cried; And all her anger woke
drewLazarus: When I said I loved her more than any other woman, she said "more than others, yes, more than others," and remained sulky

pope: 'While here I live, I leave you not,' I said to calm her fearsShe cried, 'There, then, I read your thought'; And straight dissolved in tears
drewLazarus: When I said I would never part from her in this life her eyes were filled with tears

drewLazarus: His love will increase though it may (at first seem to) fade through the short-lived distress caused by (my) dislike

drewLazarus: Is there a celestial land that can please like the feigned dislike of those whose union resembles that of earth and water?

drewLazarus: In prolonged dislike after an embrace there is a weapon that can break my heart
